intro.headline: A program is a list of statements. That's it.
intro.body:
Aktion looks like JavaScript because it *is* a strict subset of it — `function`, `if`, arrow functions, object literals, all the operators you already know. What it adds is a rule about where the UI comes from.

Every program renders from one place: `$app(...)`. The runtime streams your statements in, top to bottom, committing each line the moment it arrives — so the page shell appears before its contents finish loading.

In this world you will write a complete, valid Aktion program without learning a single new keyword.
objectives: Find the render root in any program
Build a component tree with `Column` and `Text`
Order a program so the shell streams first
Spot the two roots that *look* right and aren't
Write a valid program from an empty file

stages.title: The one entry point
stages.goal: Every Aktion program renders from exactly one $app(...).

teach.text:
There is no `main`, no `export default`, no `ReactDOM.render`. There is `$app(...)`, and there is **exactly one per program**.

Whatever you pass it becomes the page. It accepts a single node, an array of nodes rendered as siblings, or several nodes as separate arguments.

Everything else in the file — variables, functions, effects — exists to feed that one call.

code.src:
$app(Text("Hello, Aktion"))

$app([Text("one"), Text("two")])

$app(Text("one"), Text("two"))
code.caption: three ways to call it, one per program

tips: `$app` is a *builtin*, not a component — it never appears inside a tree.

tips.text: `aktion = Column([...])` is the pre-0.5 root form. The parser still tolerates it, so the validator stays silent — but nothing renders.

challenge.title: Which line renders the page?
challenge.prompt: One of these puts UI on the screen. The other three are ordinary statements that happen to build components.

options.detail: A perfectly valid statement — it just names a tree.
The legacy root form. Parses, renders nothing.
There is no `render` in Aktion.

hints: Three of these are assignments. Only one is a call to a builtin.
Look for the `$` sigil — builtins always carry it.
stages.explain: `$app(...)` is the reserved entry point and the only thing that mounts UI. `page = ...` builds a tree and parks it under a name — useful, but inert until `$app` receives it. `aktion = ...` is the pre-0.5 root that the parser still accepts, which makes it the most dangerous of the three: it validates cleanly and renders nothing.

codex.def: The reserved render root. Exactly one per program; whatever you pass it becomes the page.

stages.title: Trees, not markup
stages.goal: Build UI by nesting component calls inside arrays.

teach.text:
There is no JSX and no template syntax. A UI is a **function call whose arguments are more function calls**.

Containers take an array of children. Leaves take their content. That is the entire composition model:

code.src:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Inbox"),
  Card([
    Text("3 unread"),
    Button("Mark all read")
  ])
]))
code.caption: arrays nest as deep as you like

parts.text: the one call that mounts the page
stacks its children vertically
children always arrive as an array
a container inside a container — no depth limit

tips: PascalCase names are components; they return trees.
Reach for a pattern composite like `PageHeader` before hand-building the same thing out of `Row` + `Text`.

stages.title: Shell first, leaves later
stages.goal: Put $app(...) at the top and reference names defined below it.

teach.text:
The renderer commits each statement **as it streams in**. So the order you write things changes what the user sees first.

Names resolve from the whole top-level scope, not from source order — so `$app` can reference a `header` that is defined ten lines further down. That is the point: call `$app(...)` first and the page shell appears immediately, then each detail fills in as its line arrives.

Writing `$app` last means the user stares at nothing until the entire program has downloaded.

code.src:
$app(Column([header, stats, table]))

header = PageHeader("Orders")
stats  = Stats([StatCard("Revenue", { value: "$48k" })])
table  = Card([Text("…")])
code.caption: forward references are the idiom, not a hack

columns.title: Root last
columns.note: Nothing on screen until the last line lands.

columns.title: Root first
columns.note: Shell paints immediately; leaves attach as they arrive.

tips.text: This is a *streaming* concern, not a correctness one. Both orders produce the same final page — one just feels instant.

challenge.title: Order the program
challenge.prompt: Arrange these four statements so the page shell commits as early as possible, then each section fills in.

hints: Which single line is the one the reconciler needs before it can attach anything?
After the root, keep the sections in the order they appear on screen.
stages.explain: Hoisting is what makes this work — references resolve from the entire top-level scope, so `$app` naming `header` before `header` exists is not a forward-declaration trick, it's the normal way to write Aktion. Root first gives the reconciler a shell to attach streamed leaves to.

codex.def: Statements commit as they arrive. Call $app(...) first and forward-reference the sections below it so the shell paints immediately.

stages.title: Root Lock
stages.goal: Feel the streaming rule instead of reading it.

teach.text:
Statements are falling. The bar at the bottom is the render root.

**Catch `$app(page)` before anything else.** A leaf that lands before the shell has nothing to attach to — which is exactly what happens in a real program when you put `$app` last.

Once the root is locked, bank five more statements to clear the stage.
tips: Move the mouse — or drag on a touch screen — to slide the bar.

challenge.prompt: Catch `$app(page)` first, then bank five more statements. Anything you catch before the root ends the run.
challenge.note: Move the pointer to slide the render root. Missed statements just fall away — only order matters.

options.label: The parser requires it.
options.detail: It does not; $app can sit anywhere.

hints: The gold chip is the root. Everything cyan is a leaf.
Miss the root on purpose if you have to — it comes back around.
stages.explain: In a real streaming render this is exactly the failure: `$app` arrives last, so every earlier statement is a component with nowhere to mount, and the user watches a blank page until the final byte. Root first, always.

codex.def: The renderer attaches each statement the moment it parses, so the shell must arrive before the leaves that hang off it.

stages.title: The root that isn't
stages.goal: Recognise the two roots that validate but render nothing.

teach.text:
The schema validator is good at unknown props and misspelled components. It is powerless against a program that is *structurally fine and semantically wrong*.

Two failures produce a completely blank page with a completely clean validator:

- **`aktion = ...`** — the pre-0.5 root binding. Still parses. Never renders.
- **A component with no `return`** — the body runs, builds nothing, renders nothing.

Both of these are silent. When a page is mysteriously empty, check for them first.

infographic.title: Silent failures
rows: Two roots — only one program allowed

tips.text: A missing `return` is the single most common cause of "my component disappeared".

challenge.title: Find the silent failure
challenge.prompt: This program validates cleanly and renders an empty page. Tap the token responsible.

hints: Both bugs are here, but only one is the token that stops *anything at all* from mounting.
Ask which name the runtime actually looks for when it decides what to render.
stages.explain: `aktion = ...` is the pre-0.5 root form. The parser tolerates it for backwards compatibility, so nothing complains — but the runtime mounts `$app(...)` and only `$app(...)`, so the page stays empty. (The missing `return` in `Greeting` is a real second bug; fix that too, and note that it would have cost you only that one component instead of the whole page.)

codex.def: `aktion = ...` is the pre-0.5 render root. It still parses, so the validator stays quiet — but only `$app(...)` mounts.

stages.title: From an empty file
stages.goal: Write a complete, valid Aktion program with no scaffold.

teach.text:
Everything you need is now on the table: one root, nested calls, arrays for children.

Write a program that renders a page with a heading and a line of body text. Any components from the library are fair game — `PageHeader`, `Card`, `Text`, `Button`, `Callout` all work — as long as the whole thing hangs off a single `$app(...)`.

If the real Aktion language service is reachable, it will check your program for real and print its diagnostics under the editor.

$app(Column([
  PageHeader("…"),
  Text("…")
]))
code.caption: the shape, not the answer

mustWhy: Nothing renders without $app(...) — start there.
The two pieces need a Column([ ... ]) to stack them.
Add a PageHeader with a title string.

`Column` takes one argument: an array.
`$app(Column([PageHeader("…"), Text("…")]))` — fill in the strings.

outro.headline: You can write Aktion now
outro.body: One root, nested calls, arrays for children, shell first. Everything else in this arcade is behaviour layered onto that shape.

intro.headline: One sigil is the whole reactivity system
intro.body:
Aktion has no `useState`, no `ref()`, no store to register and no re-render call. It has one rule: **a name that starts with `$` is reactive**.

Write `$count = 0` and every part of the tree that read `$count` updates the instant you write to it. `let`, `const` and `var` are all allowed in front and all change *nothing* — they are decoration on a naming rule.

This world is about making that state move: click handlers, named actions, inputs that bind themselves without a handler, and where an atom lives when you want two copies instead of one.

stages.title: One sigil, one rule
stages.goal: Declare reactive state with $name = value — and know why let and const change nothing.

teach.text:
Aktion has exactly one kind of reactive state: `$name = value`. There is nothing to import, nothing to wrap and no setter to remember.

You read and write it with the **same sigil**. `$count` is the value; `$count = 5` is the write. No `.value` unwrapping, no `setCount`.

`let`, `const` and `var` are all accepted in front of a declaration and all change **nothing** — `const $mode = "dark"` is still reactive and still writable. The `$` is the mechanism; the keyword is decoration.

Writes are tracked by path, so `$user.role = "editor"` only re-renders the parts of the tree that actually read `.role`.

code.src:
$count = 0
$user = { name: "Ada", role: "admin" }

$count = $count + 1
$user.role = "editor"
code.caption: declare, then read and write under the same name

infographic.title: What the runtime actually sees
rows: Reactive atom — readers re-render on every write
Plain binding — evaluated once, never re-renders

tips: Path-level tracking is an atom-only privilege: it applies to `$name = value`, not to hook setters or resource bags.

tips.text: `count = 0` is not an error. It is a perfectly good plain binding — it simply never updates the UI, and nothing warns you.

challenge.title: Which one is reactive?
challenge.prompt: Four ways a developer might reach for state on their first day. Only one of them is something the UI will re-render for.

options.detail: Valid Aktion — a plain binding. `let` does not make anything reactive.
There is no `useState` in Aktion.
No wrapper object. Reactivity is a naming rule, not a proxy.

hints: Three of these come from another framework or declare an ordinary value.
Look at the first character of the name, not the keyword in front of it.
stages.explain: The `$` prefix is not a convention that a linter enforces — it is what the planner looks for when it decides which names to track. That is exactly why `let count = 0` is legal and inert while `let $count = 0` is reactive: the keyword is thrown away, the sigil is not. And because reads and writes use the same name, there is no setter to keep in sync and no stale-closure class of bug to reason about.

codex.def: The one reactive atom. The `$` prefix — not `let`/`const`/`var` — is what makes a name reactive; read and write it with the same sigil.

stages.title: Wire the click
stages.goal: Hand a lambda to onClick and write state from inside it.

teach.text:
An event handler is not special machinery. It is an ordinary prop holding an ordinary function. `Button` has `onClick`; give it a lambda and put the write inside.

Inside any imperative body — a lambda, an action, an effect — the **full assignment operator set** is available: `=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `??=`, `++`, `--`. So `$count += 1` and `$count = $count + 1` are the same statement.

Reading the atom back into the tree needs no subscription. `Text(`Count: ${$count}`)` re-renders on every write purely because it mentioned `$count`.

code.src:
$count = 0

$app(Card([
  Text(`Count: ${$count}`, { variant: "title" }),
  Button("+1", { onClick: () => $count += 1, variant: "primary" })
]))
code.caption: the whole counter — six lines, no wiring

parts.text: the label — the one bare argument in a canonical call
wants a callable; lives in the trailing options object
an imperative body, so assignment operators are legal inside
identical to $count = $count + 1
everything non-positional shares that one object

tips: `onClick` is the canonical prop name; the older `action` alias is still accepted.

tips.text: `Button("+1", () => $count += 1)` also works — the second positional slot *is* `onClick`. But `Button("+1", "primary")` drops a string into that same slot: no handler, no variant, no complaint.

challenge.title: Complete the counter

hints: The bare positional argument of a `Button` is its label.
The prop is the DOM event name in camelCase — nothing is renamed.

stages.explain: A handler is a prop whose value happens to be callable, which is why a lambda, a named action and `() => doTwoThings()` all fit the same slot with no adapter. And because a lambda body is an imperative body, the compound operators are open to you: `$count += 1` compiles to `$count = $count + 1` and notifies every reader of `$count`. `count += 1` would compile fine too — and update nothing, because `count` was never an atom.

codex.def: A prop holding a callable. Any lambda or named action fits; inside the body you may write atoms with =, +=, -=, ??=, ++ and friends.

    Button("Reset", { onClick: () => $count = 0, variant: "secondary" })
  ])
]))

stages.title: Name it, don't call it
stages.goal: Declare a camelCase action once and hand it to a handler by name.

teach.text:
A `function` with a camelCase name is an **action**: a callable that does something, with an optional `return`. Case is only a readability convention — what decides its role is where you use it.

There are two ways to use one. As a handler, pass the **name**: `onClick: save`. As an expression, call it: `$greeting = greet("Ada")`.

Actions are where imperative work belongs — several writes at once, and the feedback that goes with them. `$toast.success`, `$toast.error`, `$toast.info` and `$toast.warning` render their own stacked layer, so you never add a toast component to the tree.

Need to pass an argument to a handler? Wrap it in a lambda: `onClick: () => remove(item.id)`.

code.src:
$draft = ""
$saved = ""

function save() {
  $saved = $draft
  $draft = ""
  $toast.success("Draft saved")
}

$app(Card([
  Input("draft", { value: $draft, placeholder: "Write something" }),
  Buttons([Button("Save", { onClick: save, variant: "primary" })])
]))
code.caption: declare once, hand it over by name

columns.title: Called while the tree is built
columns.note: The object literal is evaluated now, so save() runs now and the button receives whatever it returned.

columns.title: Handed over
columns.note: The button holds the function and calls it when the user clicks.

tips: An action may `return` a value, which is what lets you use the same declaration as an expression: `$greeting = greet("Ada")`.
`$toast` is one of exactly five namespaces — `$util`, `$storage`, `$console`, `$toast`, `$dom`.

stages.explain: `onClick` wants a callable, and an object literal is evaluated the moment the tree is built — not when the user clicks. So `save` puts the function in the slot, while `save()` runs the action right there during render and stores its return value, which is usually nothing: the side effect fires at the wrong time *and* the button ends up with no handler. A string and a number are not callable either. Wrapping in a lambda is how you delay a call you need to pass arguments to: `onClick: () => remove(id)`.

codex.def: A camelCase `function name(args) { … }` — a callable effect with an optional return. Pass it to a handler by name (`onClick: save`), or call it as an expression (`$x = greet("Ada")`).

stages.title: Sigil Storm
stages.goal: Sort names by the only thing that decides.

teach.text:
Names fall down the middle, one at a time. Steer each one into the bin it belongs in.

**Left is reactive. Right is inert.** A name is reactive if — and only if — it starts with `$`. `let $draft` goes left. `const rows` goes right. The keyword in front is noise every single time, and that is the whole point of the run.

Eight sorted correctly clears the stage. Three misfiles ends it.
tips: Move the pointer left or right to steer the falling name.

A plain binding — evaluated once.

stages.explain: Every run of this drills one decision: the sigil, and nothing else. It matters because the failure is silent — `let count = 0` and `let $count = 0` look almost identical in a diff, both validate, and only one of them makes the page move. When a value in Aktion mysteriously refuses to update, the first thing to check is whether it ever carried the `$`.

codex.def: Only a `$`-prefixed name (or a member chain rooted at one) is tracked. `let`/`const`/`var` never affect it — a plain name is a one-shot binding.

stages.title: Bound both ways
stages.goal: Wire an input to state with no handler at all.

teach.text:
Pass a `$variable` as an input's `value` and the runtime wires it **both ways**: typing writes the atom, writing the atom updates the field. No handler, no `e.target.value`, no controlled-component ceremony.

A member chain rooted at an atom behaves the same way, so `value: $profile.email` binds one field of one object — and only the readers of `.email` re-render.

The binding is a consequence of *what you passed*, not of a special prop. Put a plain string in that slot and the field renders it and drops every keystroke.

`onChange(value)` is still there when you need to *do* something as well as store it. It receives the new value directly — already unwrapped — and works alongside a binding or instead of one.

code.caption: not one handler in the file

code2.caption: onChange receives the value, not an event

tips: `Input`, `Select`, `Checkbox`, `Switch`, `Slider`, `MultiSelect`, `CheckBoxGroup`, `DatePicker` and the rest of the form group all bind this way.

tips.text: `value: "ada@example.com"` is a literal, not an address. The field shows it, the user types over it, and nothing is stored.

challenge.prompt: One token in this call is both *read* and *written* by the runtime. Click the marker sitting on it.

the prop name — a plain literal would fit here too

Three of these markers sit on things that would be identical if the field were read-only.

stages.explain: Binding is not a prop, a directive or a modifier — it is inferred from the argument. When the value in an input slot is an atom, or a member chain rooted at one, the runtime has an address it can write to, so it installs the write for you. Hand it a literal and there is nowhere to put the keystroke. That is also why `onChange` is genuinely optional here: it is a notification, not the storage mechanism, and it hands you the value already unwrapped so there is no `e.target.value` to remember.

codex.def: Passing a `$atom` (or a member chain rooted at one) as an input's `value` wires reads and writes both ways — no handler required. `onChange(value)` is optional and additive.

stages.title: Two counters, two states
stages.goal: Give a component its own private state and prove it by rendering two.

teach.text:
Where you declare an atom decides who shares it.

At the **top level**, `$count = 0` is one atom for the whole program. Every reader and every writer touches the same value.

Inside a **component body**, `$n = 0` is a declaration *per instance*. Two call sites get two independent atoms: the initializer runs once when that instance first mounts, and later re-renders keep whatever has been written since.

Write a `Counter(label)` that holds its own count, then render two of them side by side. If they move together, the atom is in the wrong place.

code.caption: one atom per call site — the shape, not the answer

layers.label: $total = 0
layers.note: top level — one atom, shared by every reader in the program

layers.label: Counter("Left")
layers.note: its own $n, from the same line of source

layers.label: Counter("Right")
layers.note: its own $n — a second instance, a second atom

tips: Always end a component with an explicit `return`. A body that falls through renders nothing, silently.

tips.text: Instance identity comes from the call site. When siblings can reorder, pin it with the universal `{ key: id }` prop — every component call accepts one — so each instance keeps hold of its own atom.

challenge.title: Write it yourself
challenge.prompt: Write a `Counter(label)` component that declares its own count atom, renders the label with the count, and has a `+1` button. Then render **two** of them in a `Row`, all under one `$app(...)`.

mustWhy: Start with `function Counter(label) { … }`.
Declare the count atom inside the body — `$n = 0`.
A component that never returns renders nothing.
The `+1` button needs an `onClick` that writes the atom.
Render two counters so you can see that they are independent.
Nothing renders without `$app(...)`.

hints: The atom goes on the first line of the body, before the `return`.
`$n += 1` inside the lambda is enough — no props, no store, no context.
`$app(Row([Counter("Left"), Counter("Right")]))` — build the component above it.
stages.explain: The rule is *where*, not *how*. The very same statement means two different things depending on its position: at the top level it declares one shared atom, inside a component body it declares one atom per instance. That is why `Counter("Left")` and `Counter("Right")` count separately with no props, no context and no store — and why lifting that one line out to the top level would silently make both buttons drive the same number. Choosing the scope *is* the state-management decision in Aktion; there is no second API for it.

games.title: Component Forge
games.subtitle: Your own components, and the argument trap

intro.headline: A component is a function that returns a tree
intro.body:
There is no component class, no registration step, and no `props` object. You write an ordinary JavaScript function, its parameters are ordinary parameters with ordinary defaults, and whatever it `return`s becomes UI.

That simplicity moves the difficulty somewhere unexpected: to the **call site**. Because arguments can be passed by position *or* by name, one call can be structurally perfect and semantically wrong — and the validator will not say a word.

`Button("Save", "primary")` is that call. This world is about writing components, and about never being fooled by that line again.
intro.codeCaption: declare it, then call it two different ways
objectives: Declare a component with real JS parameters and defaults
End every component with an explicit `return`
Choose one of the three call forms and stay inside it
Say where `"primary"` lands in `Button("Save", "primary")`
Extend a built-in component instead of replacing it

stages.title: Declare and return
stages.goal: A component is a function whose return value is a tree.

teach.text:
`function Name(params) { return Tree }`. That is the entire declaration syntax. No decorator, no `defineComponent`, no export.

The rule that catches everyone is the last word of it: **always end with an explicit `return`**. A body that builds a `Badge(...)` and then falls off the end really did build the node — and then discarded it. Nothing throws, nothing warns, the page is just missing a piece.

The mirror-image mistake is returning the name instead of a call. `return Badge` hands back the function itself; the renderer has no instruction to invoke it, so again: nothing.

code.caption: declaration, parameters, return — nothing else is required

infographic.title: What the last statement decides
rows: nothing — the node is built, then dropped
nothing — a bare name is a value, not a call

tips: Case is a readability convention only. `function chip(...)` renders exactly the same as `function Chip(...)`.

tips.text: A component with no `return` renders nothing and reports nothing. Check for it first whenever a component vanishes.

challenge.title: Four Chips, four outcomes
challenge.prompt: All four of these declare something called `Chip`. Exactly one puts a pill on the screen; the other three are silent no-ops, and no two of them fail the same way. Match each declaration to what it actually does.

right.label: A pill on the page — the node is built and then escapes the body
The node really is built, then dropped when the body ends
The component itself is handed back, and the renderer never calls it
A plain object — there is no registry to declare a component to

hints: Two of the four really do build a Badge node. Only one of those hands it back.
A component is a function. What must a function do for a value to escape its body?
Pair the one that works first, then separate the other three by *why* they fail: no `return`, a name instead of a call, or not a function at all.
stages.explain: A component is not a special kind of object — it is a plain function whose return value happens to be a tree. That is exactly why the missing `return` is invisible: the body ran, `Badge(...)` really did produce a node, and then the function ended and threw it away. Nothing is wrong enough to report. `return Badge` fails for the mirror reason: a bare name is the function itself, and the renderer never calls what it is handed. And the object-literal form has no meaning at all here — with no component registry, an object named `Chip` is just an object.

afterCode.caption: the shape to remember

codex.def: `function Name(p) { return Tree }` — a plain JS function that returns a component tree. No `return` means no output and no error.

stages.title: The signature is the API
stages.goal: Props are real JS parameters with real JS defaults — there is no props object.

teach.text:
Because a call site is an ordinary function call, the parameters are ordinary parameters. Give them JavaScript defaults with `=`, destructure them if you like, and read them by name inside the body.

There is nothing to reach into: `props.tone` cannot work because nothing ever builds a `props`. Read the parameter list and you know every prop the component takes and which one is positional.

State declared inside the body belongs to the *instance*, not the program. `$n = 0` in a component body is a declaration: the initializer runs once when that instance mounts, and every later re-render keeps whatever the user, an action, or an effect has written since.

code.caption: plain params, JS defaults, destructuring — all standard

code2.caption: two call sites, two independent $n atoms

infographic.title: Reading a signature
infographic.code: function Chip(label, tone = "neutral") { return Badge(label, { tone }) }

parts.text: Case is convention. What makes it a component is that it returns a tree.
Real JS parameters. There is no props object to reach into.
A plain JS default, used whenever the caller omits that argument.
Leave this off and the component renders nothing, silently.

tips: Destructured parameters work: `function Panel({ title, tone = "info" })` is a valid signature.

tips.text: `$n = 0` inside a body is a declaration, not an assignment that runs on every render. Two call sites get two independent atoms.

challenge.title: Declare it, then call it
challenge.prompt: Three slots: give `tone` a default, let the tree out, and call the component you just declared. Four of the chips are habits from other frameworks — leave them in the bank.

hints: Parameters are ordinary JavaScript. How do you give an ordinary JS parameter a default?
There is no props object — `label` and `tone` are already in scope inside the body.
The last slot sits in call position. It needs the name declared at the top of the file.
stages.explain: There is no props object because there is no framework layer standing between the call and the function — `Chip("Shipped", "success")` is just a call, so `label` and `tone` are just parameters and `= "neutral"` is just a JavaScript default. `default:` and `props.` are shapes from Vue and React that have nothing to bind to here. The payoff is that a component's signature is its complete, readable API: no separate prop declaration can drift out of sync with it.

codex.def: Component props are real JS parameters with real JS defaults (`tone = "neutral"`). There is no props object; destructured parameters work too.

preview.caption: the third pill never passed a tone — it took the default

stages.title: One call, one form
stages.goal: Pick one of the three argument forms per call, and know what position binds.

teach.text:
Every call picks exactly one of three forms:

- **canonical** — `Component(positional, { prop: value })`
- **all-positional** — `Component(a, b, c)`, binding in signature order
- **all-named** — `Component({ prop: value })`

All-positional is the sharp one. An unnamed argument binds to the *next prop in the signature*, whatever that happens to be. `Badge(label, tone, icon, size)` puts tone second, so `Badge("Live", "success")` is correct. `Button(label, onClick, variant, type, size, …)` puts **onClick** second — so `Button("Save", "primary")` hands the string to the click handler, renders the default style, and validates cleanly.

Never split one object between the two roles. Some components take a *leading* props object because their children are the trailing positional — `Grid({ columns: 12 }, [CardA(), CardB()])` — but that is still one form, not a mix of two.

code.src:
Button("Save", { variant: "primary" })      // canonical
StatCard("Revenue", "$48k", "up")           // all-positional
Button({ label: "Save", variant: "primary" }) // all-named
code.caption: three forms, three calls — never two forms in one call

columns.title: Slot two is onClick
columns.note: Signature: label, onClick, variant. "primary" becomes the handler — default styling, dead click, clean validator.

columns.title: Named, so order stops mattering
columns.note: One positional, every other prop named in the trailing object.

tips: All-positional is safe only when the props you want are adjacent and leading — `StatCard("Revenue", "$48k", "up")` is fine.

tips.text: Never split one object between the two roles. One call, one form.

challenge.prompt: Every one of these passes the validator. Switch ON only the calls where each argument actually lands on the prop the author meant.
challenge.help: Read the signature in your head before you flip anything. Leave the misrouted calls off.

switches.detail: canonical: one positional, every other prop in the trailing object

switches.label: Button("Save", "primary")
switches.detail: Button(label, onClick, variant, …)

switches.label: Badge("Live", "success")
switches.detail: Badge(label, tone, icon, size)

switches.label: Button({ label: "Save", variant: "primary" })
switches.detail: all-named: one object, every prop by name

switches.label: StatCard("Revenue", "up")
switches.detail: StatCard(label, value, trend, delta, …)

switches.label: Grid({ columns: 3 }, [Card([Text("A")]), Card([Text("B")])])
switches.detail: leading props object, children as the trailing positional

hints: For each call, say the signature out loud and ask what prop slot two is.
`Button(label, onClick, variant, …)` versus `Badge(label, tone, …)`. Only one of those makes a second positional string safe.
`StatCard(label, value, trend, …)` — a two-argument call never reaches `trend`.
stages.explain: Position is meaningful, so an unnamed argument binds to whatever prop comes next in the declaration order — nothing about the string `"primary"` marks it as a variant. `Badge("Live", "success")` and `Button("Save", "primary")` are structurally identical calls; only the two signatures differ, and that difference is the whole bug. `StatCard("Revenue", "up")` fails the same way one slot earlier: the tile renders with the value "up" and no trend. The canonical form exists precisely to make a call immune to its signature's order — name the prop and position stops mattering.

codex.def: `C(positional, { props })`, `C(a, b, c)` in signature order, or `C({ props })`. Pick one per call; never split an object between the two roles.

stages.title: The Forge
stages.goal: Route every argument token into the role that actually binds it.

teach.text:
A call site is being forged: `Button(  __  , {  __  })`. Argument tokens are falling into it.

**Tap a lane to route the lowest token.** A token that carries its own name (`variant: "primary"`) belongs in the options object. The label `"Save"` belongs in the positional slot.

The bare `"primary"` belongs in neither. Send it to the positional lane and you will watch it wire itself to `onClick`. Let it fall instead — it only becomes a variant once you give it its name back.
tips: Anything with a colon in it is a named prop.

tips.text: Three misroutes ends the run. Letting a token fall costs nothing.

challenge.title: Route the tokens

challenge.note: Tap a lane at the bottom to route the lowest falling token.
challenge.winNote: Press Check to bank the XP.

options.label: Into the second positional slot — which the signature declares as `onClick`.
Into `variant`, but `"primary"` is not a valid variant value.
options.detail: `"primary"` is a perfectly valid variant. It simply never reached that prop.

options.label: Nowhere — arguments past the first are ignored unless they are named.
options.detail: Nothing is ignored. Every positional argument binds to the next prop in the signature.

options.label: Into `type`, the third prop in the signature.
options.detail: Off by one — the order is label, onClick, variant, type.

hints: A colon means the token names its own destination.
The bare `"primary"` has no home in this call. Do nothing and it falls away for free.
Tap the lane, not the token — the lowest token is the one that gets routed.
stages.explain: Routing is the whole model. A token that carries a name can sit anywhere inside the options object, because the name — not the position — decides what it binds to. A token with no name is bound by position alone, so it lands wherever the signature says the next slot is. That is why `"primary"` on its own has nowhere to go in a `Button` call: as a positional it becomes the click handler, and inside an object it is not a key/value pair at all. Giving it back its name is the entire fix.

codex.def: An unnamed argument binds to the next prop in the component's signature — so `Button("Save", "primary")` sets onClick, not variant.

stages.title: The prop that wasn't
stages.goal: Spot a named prop that quietly became a positional argument.

teach.text:
When you call **your own** component with a trailing object, the runtime has to decide what that object is: a bag of named props, or just a value you happen to be passing.

Its rule is mechanical. If any key in the object matches a parameter name, it is treated as named props. If **no** key matches, the whole object is forwarded as a positional argument instead.

That rule is what makes an opaque data payload or a slots bag work at all. The price is that a misspelled prop name is not an error — it is a differently shaped argument, arriving in the next positional slot. Built-in components validate their prop names, so a typo there is caught; your own components have no prop list to check against.

code.caption: one wrong letter, no diagnostic

infographic.title: How the trailing object is classified

steps.label: not a props bag
steps.note: so it is a value, not named props

tips.text: This flip applies to *your* components. Built-ins reject unknown prop names outright — `Badge("Live", { tint: "success" })` is a validation error.

tips: The runtime's strict mode logs a warning when it forwards an unmatched object. The default mode stays silent.

challenge.title: It renders. It is still wrong.
challenge.prompt: Every pill appears, nothing throws, the validator is clean — and one badge has lost its colour. Tap the token responsible.

hints: The program renders and nothing throws. So look for a name that matches nothing.
Check every key of an options object against the parameter list directly above it.
`tone` is a parameter of `Chip`. Is `tint`?
stages.explain: The runtime cannot tell a props bag from a payload by shape alone, so it uses the only signal available: do the keys name parameters? `tint` names neither `label` nor `tone`, so the object is classified as a value and slides into the second positional slot — `tone` becomes `{ tint: "success" }`, and `Badge` receives an object where a tone string belongs. The other three spans are all legal on purpose: `Chip("Refunded", "danger")` is an all-positional call, `Chip("Paid")` takes the default, and `Badge` inside the body is just the library component. This is the cost of the rule that lets you pass an opaque slots object at all — and it is why a prop typo on your own components is worth reading for twice.

codex.def: If a trailing object's keys match none of a custom component's parameters, it is forwarded as a positional argument instead of raising an error.

stages.title: Extend, don't replace
stages.goal: Wrap a built-in component by reusing its own name.

teach.text:
Declaring a component with a built-in's name is normally rejected — a program containing two different `Badge`s is unreadable. There is exactly one exception, and it is the useful one.

**If the body calls that same name, the declaration is a wrapper.** Inside its own body, the name resolves to the *built-in*, so the outermost call is yours and the innermost is the library's. It extends instead of recursing, and it terminates at depth one.

Write a `Badge` that pins every pill to the success tone, then render two of them. Same call sites everywhere else in the program — new behaviour.

layers.label: Badge(label, { tone: "success" })

layers.label: the library pill
layers.note: renders once — no recursion

tips: A `function` declared inside another component's body is scoped to it — component-local helpers never leak to the rest of the program.

tips.text: The exception is narrow. Reuse a built-in's name *only* when your body calls that same name; any other shadowing is a validator error.

The body has to call `Badge(...)` — that inner call is what makes it a wrapper instead of an error.
Pin the tone in the trailing object: `{ tone: "success" }`.

Inside the body of `function Badge(...)`, the name `Badge` means the library one.
`function Badge(label) { return Badge(label, { tone: "success" }) }`, then call it twice inside `$app(Column([...]))`.
stages.explain: The validator's rule is a readability rule, not a technical limit: a shadowing declaration is rejected unless its body calls the shadowed name, because that pattern is unmistakably a wrapper rather than a replacement. The runtime cooperates by resolving the name to the built-in while it is evaluating the declaration's own body, which is what stops the wrapper recursing to the depth limit. A renamed wrapper — `SuccessBadge` — works equally well and is often clearer; the reason to keep the name is that every existing call site inherits the new behaviour with no edits.

outro.body: A component is a function that returns a tree, its parameters are its API, and every call picks one form and stays in it. `Button("Save", "primary")` will not fool you twice — and neither will a trailing object whose keys match nothing.

games.title: Layout Architect
games.subtitle: Dense, production-grade pages in one line each

intro.headline: Stop building sections. Start placing them.
intro.body:
Most layout code is people rebuilding the same four things: a page title with actions, a strip of numbers, a filter bar, a board. Aktion ships those as **pattern composites** — one call each, already dense, already responsive, already themed.

Underneath them are the primitives: `Column`, `Row`, `Grid` and a small cast of wrappers. You need them, but you should reach for them *second*. A page hand-composed out of `Card` and `Stack` reads as a wireframe; the same page built from composites reads as a product.

This world is the difference between a screen that validates and a screen that looks finished.
intro.code:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Engineering Q3", { subtitle: "12 active · 4 at risk" }),
  Toolbar({ searchable: true, right: [Button("New project", { variant: "primary" })] }),
  Stats([
    StatCard("Active", { value: "12" }),
    StatCard("At risk", { value: "4", trend: "up", delta: "+2", tone: "warning" })
  ]),
  Card([
    SectionHeader("Recent activity"),
    Timeline([TimelineItem("Order #1204 shipped", { time: "2h ago", icon: "truck", tone: "success" })])
  ])
], { gap: "lg" }))

layers.label: AppShell · Container · Section
layers.note: the surface the page sits on

layers.label: PageHeader · Stats · Toolbar · KanbanBoard
layers.note: composites — one call, one whole section

layers.label: Column · Row · Grid
layers.note: primitives — the glue between sections

layers.label: Card · Box · Separator · Spacer

objectives: Pick `Column`, `Row` or `Grid` without thinking twice
Commit a whole page section with one composite call
Tell `Badge` from `Pill`, and `Callout` from `CardSection`
Make a layout responsive with `{ base, md, lg }` and nothing else
Ship a page dense enough that it looks designed

stages.title: Three primitives, one job each
stages.goal: Pick Column, Row or Grid on reflex — and know the one case that needs Stack.

teach.text:
Three containers do almost all the work. `Column` stacks children top to bottom and stretches them to full width — the default shape of a page body and of a card body. `Row` lays them left to right, keeps every child at its **natural** width, and centres them vertically. `Grid` gives cells that share one width.

`Stack` is the low-level flex box underneath both. Reach for it only when the *direction itself* has to change across breakpoints — because a `row` Stack grows its children equally by default (`uniform` is true for row stacks). Hand it a search field and two buttons and you get three identical thirds.

Spacing is a token, never a pixel: `none · 3xs · 2xs · xs · sm · md · lg · xl · 2xl · 3xl`. The rhythm that reads as designed is `lg` between top-level sections, `md` inside a card, `sm` between tightly related controls.

The rest of the set fills the gaps: `Center` for both-axis centring, `Container` for a readable max width, `Box` when a `Card` is too heavy, `Section` for a full-bleed page band, `Split` for two panes, `Spacer()` to push siblings apart, `Separator` to draw a line.

Column([header, kpis, table], { gap: "lg" })

Row([SearchBar("q"), Spacer(), Button("New order")], { gap: "sm" })

Grid(cards, { columns: 4, gap: "md" })

Make one child of a `Row` expand with `StackItem(child, { grow: 1 })`; a bare `Spacer()` between two children pushes them to opposite edges.

challenge.title: What each call actually renders
challenge.prompt: Five calls, five different shapes on screen. Match each one to what it really puts in front of the user.

right.label: The field at its own natural width, the button shoved to the far right edge
One line, two identical halves — the field comes out as wide as the button

Only one call in the left column is documented as 'natural width, vertically centred'.
`Spacer()` between two children is what pushes them to opposite edges. A `direction` on a `Column` does nothing at all.

One call names a prop its component does not have — and renders exactly as if you had left it off.
stages.explain: `Row` exists precisely so children keep their natural size — a search field stays a search field, a button stays button-sized. `Stack` in `row` mode is the same flex box with `uniform` defaulting to true, which is the whole reason `Row` is a separate component. `Grid(columns: 3)` asks for equal thirds out loud, and `Column` never flows horizontally no matter what you pass it. Same short cast of children, five completely different shapes.

stages.title: One call, one whole section
stages.goal: Reach for a pattern composite before you open a single Card.

teach.text:
Before you compose anything by hand, check whether the library already owns the idiom. `PageHeader` is a page title with breadcrumbs, a status slot and an actions row. `Stats` is a KPI strip. `Toolbar` is a search-and-filters bar. `EmptyState`, `Timeline`, `DescriptionList`, `KanbanBoard`, `FeatureGrid`, `PricingTable`, `Hero`, `SectionHeader` — each of them commits a finished visual section in one line.

They are not shortcuts. They are tuned: spacing rhythm, responsive behaviour, iconography, heading levels and semantic tone all come with them. A hand-rolled equivalent gets none of that and will drift away from every other page in the app.

The rule of thumb for how many sections a page needs: a dashboard wants **six** named sections, a detail, settings, list or landing page wants **five**. Two components stacked vertically is a wireframe, not a product — if a draft is short, add a complementary section rather than padding the ones you have.

PageHeader("Orders", { subtitle: "1,204 this month", actions: [Button("Export", { icon: "download" })] })

Toolbar({ searchable: true, right: [Button("New order", { variant: "primary" })] })

Stats([StatCard("Revenue", { value: "$48,120", trend: "up", delta: "+12%" })])

EmptyState("No orders yet", { description: "They land here the moment one arrives." })
code.caption: four sections, four calls

columns.title: Hand-composed
columns.note: Nine lines, no breadcrumbs, no status slot, no heading level — and it will drift from every other page.

columns.title: The composite
columns.note: One call. Breadcrumbs, the status slot and the actions row arrive with it.

tips: `Grid`, `Column` and `Row` still matter — they are the glue *between* composites, not a replacement for them.
`columns`, `gap`, `padding`, `align`, `justify` and `direction` all accept a `{ base, sm, md, lg, xl }` map instead of a value.

challenge.title: Compose the orders page
challenge.prompt: Four nodes are missing from the page tree. Three want the composite that owns that section; the fourth has to survive a 390px phone, so a bare number will not do.

hints: Three of the four slots are pattern composites — each one commits a whole section on its own.
`CardHeader` opens a card. The thing that opens a *page* has a different name.
A responsive prop takes an object keyed by breakpoint: `{ base: …, md: …, lg: … }`.
nudges: Two chips in the bank are the hand-rolled versions of composites already in the bank.
`4` is a legal value for `columns` — it is just wrong for a grid that has to reflow.
stages.explain: Every one of those three composites exists because the same section gets rebuilt on every page of every app. Using them is not laziness — it is how the pages stay consistent with each other, and how you get breadcrumbs, status slots, responsive wrapping and correct heading levels without asking. The `Grid` is the only place a primitive belongs here: it is the glue between the section composites, and a `{ base, md, lg }` map is how it survives a phone.

afterCode.caption: one column on a phone, four on a desktop

stages.title: Two chips and two bands
stages.goal: Choose between components the validator is happy to let you confuse.

teach.text:
Some components are near-identical in the prop table and completely different on screen. The schema validator accepts all of them, so this one is on you.

`Badge` is the **solid, high-attention chip** — "Recommended", "Save 50%", "Most popular". `Pill` is the **soft tinted state label** for the current state of a thing — "SSL active", "pending", "broken". Reach for `Pill` when the text describes *what something is right now*, and `Badge` when it is trying to catch an eye.

`Callout` is a standalone bordered notice that stands on its own between two sections. `CardSection` is a full-bleed tinted band that lives **inside** a `Card`, grouping and colouring part of that card's content edge to edge. If it needs its own border, it is a `Callout`; if it needs to be part of a card, it is a `CardSection`.

The same trap runs through the rest of the library: `Spinner` is a rotating ring for a whole panel, `LoadingDots` a quieter inline pulse. `Buttons` is a gapped row, `ButtonGroup` an edge-to-edge joined control, `SegmentedControl` a single-select pill track. `ActionStripe` is an always-interactive navigation row, `ListItem` a presentational row, `Tile` a grid unit.

Pill("SSL active", { tone: "success" })

Callout("Your trial ends in 3 days", { tone: "warning", description: "Add a card to keep the workspace open." })

Card([
  SectionHeader("Danger zone"),
  CardSection([Text("Deleting this project cannot be undone.")], { tone: "critical" })
])

stages.title: Blueprint
stages.goal: Fill every region of a dashboard with the composite that finishes it.

teach.text:
A dashboard wireframe is on the table. One region lights up at a time and tells you what it needs.

**Tap the composite that owns that job** before the bar runs out. Get it right and the region fills in dense — a heading bar, a body, a footer rule. Get it wrong, or run out of time, and the region renders as a single thin line: exactly what a page looks like when you hand-compose a section that already exists.

Five filled regions clears the stage. Three sparse ones ends the run.
tips: Read the *job*, not the words. "key / value summary of one record" is a `DescriptionList` even though nothing says list.

The reason the density targets in the skill exist (six sections for a dashboard, five for a detail page) is that a page reads as unfinished long before it reads as broken, and no validator will ever tell you so. The composites are how you hit those targets without writing a hundred lines.

stages.title: One layout, every viewport
stages.goal: Read a breakpoint map the way the runtime does — which props take one, and where each key takes over.

teach.text:
There is no breakpoint prop, no media-query escape hatch and no mobile variant of any component. Six layout props take a **map** wherever they take a value: `gap`, `padding`, `align`, `justify`, `columns` and `direction`.

The keys are `base`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl` — 640, 768, 1024 and 1280 pixels, with `base` as the mobile-first floor. Values cascade upwards, so a breakpoint you leave out inherits the one below it: `{ base: 1, lg: 4 }` is one column all the way to 1024px and four beyond it.

This is where `Stack` finally earns its place. It is the only primitive whose `direction` you can map, which is why a filter rail that becomes a top strip on a phone is a `Stack` and not a `Row`.

code.src: Grid(cards, { columns: { base: 1, md: 2, lg: 4 }, gap: { base: "sm", lg: "lg" } })
code.caption: one column on a phone, four on a desktop

code2.src: Stack([filters, results], { direction: { base: "column", md: "row" }, gap: "lg" })
code2.caption: stacked on a phone, side by side from 768px up

parts.text: one of the six props that take a map instead of a value
mobile-first — everything narrower than 640px gets this
takes over at md and holds until the next named key
the widest rule here, so xl inherits it too

tips: Leave breakpoints out on purpose. `{ base: 1, lg: 4 }` is usually better than spelling out all five.

tips.text: Unknown breakpoint keys are silently ignored so a typo cannot crash the page. `{ mobile: 1, desktop: 4 }` matches nothing, is treated as a plain value, and quietly gives you the component default.

challenge.title: Four columns, but when?
challenge.prompt: Five Grid calls, all of them legal, all of them asking for four columns. Order them by the viewport width at which each one first actually renders four — narrowest at the top, never at the bottom.

hints: Two of the five have no breakpoint doing any work at all: one is four columns at every width, the other is four columns at none.
`sm` is 640, `md` is 768, `lg` is 1024, `xl` is 1280 — the key names *are* the ladder, and a key you leave out inherits the one below it.
`desktop` is not one of the five keys. Nothing throws; it simply never matches, so `base` holds all the way up.
nudges: Ask of each line: at what width does that `4` first take effect — and does it ever?
A bare `columns: 4` is not a phone layout. It is four columns at 320px too.
stages.explain: The six mappable props are exactly the ones that describe space and arrangement, and the runtime turns each map into real CSS custom properties inside media queries — no JavaScript resize listener, no re-render on rotate. Props that describe what a component *is* rather than how much room it has — `variant`, `size`, or a CSS length like `minChildWidth` — take a single value and nothing else. Each key holds until the next named one takes over, which is why `{ base: 1, xl: 4 }` is one column all the way to 1280px. And because a map is just an object, the runtime cannot tell a typo'd key from a deliberate omission: it ignores what it does not recognise. That is the whole story of the last line: `base` matches and `desktop` does not, so the grid holds one column at 4K exactly as calmly as it does at 320px.

afterCode.caption: two maps, zero media queries

codex.def: `{ base, sm, md, lg, xl }` (640/768/1024/1280px) accepted by `gap`, `padding`, `align`, `justify`, `columns` and `direction`. Values cascade upwards; unrecognised keys are silently ignored.

stages.title: Ship something dense
stages.goal: Write a page with five named sections and not one hard-coded colour.

teach.text:
Two habits separate a page that looks designed from one that looks generated.

**Do not fight the defaults.** These components already guess the obvious: `StatCard("Revenue", …)` picks an icon from the label, `PageHeader(title)` derives `["Home", title]` breadcrumbs (pass `breadcrumbs: false` to suppress them), `EmptyState(title)` picks an icon from the title, `Banner(title, { tone })` picks one from the tone, and `Image(src, { ratio: "16:9" })` constrains itself with no outer `AspectRatio`. Passing what they already infer adds noise, not control.

**Never hard-code colour, spacing or typography.** Pass a semantic `tone` or `variant` — `default`, `primary`, `success`, `warning`, `danger`, `info` — and let the theme resolve it. The same program has to survive six built-in themes; a hex value survives none of them. (`tone` and `variant` are interchangeable on 41 component specs, and `children`/`child` on 57, so a plausible guess is rarely a build failure.)

Now build one. Five named sections, all of it hanging off a single `$app(...)`.

], { gap: "lg" }))

games.title: Flow Control
games.subtitle: Statements, expressions, and the line between them

intro.headline: Some code makes a value. Some code makes things happen.
intro.body:
Aktion is JavaScript, so it inherits JavaScript's oldest split: **expressions** produce a value, **statements** perform an action. In a browser you can ignore the difference for years. Here you cannot — because the right-hand side of every `=` is a value slot, and a UI is built almost entirely out of `=`.

`if`, `switch`, `for`, `while`, `do...while` and `try` are statements. They are fully supported; they simply live in one place — an imperative body. That means a `function`, a lambda written with braces, or an `$effect` callback. Put one on the right of `=` and the parser stops you and names the construct.

That sounds restrictive until you see the replacements. A ternary branches. `.map` loops. A `switch` wrapped in a function and then called does multi-way dispatch. Every one of them is shorter than what it replaces.
intro.codeCaption: the two ways to branch into a value

layers.note: bindings, $app, and imperative statements that run once per plan

layers.note: right of an equals sign, a call argument, an array element - values only

objectives: Name the six block constructs that cannot sit on the right of an `=`
Replace an `if` with a ternary and a `for` with `.map`

stages.title: Statements are not values
stages.goal: Tell an expression from a statement before the parser has to.

teach.text:
An **expression** evaluates to something: `2 + 2`, `$rows.length`, `cond ? a : b`, `Card([Text("hi")])`. Anywhere a value is expected — right of `=`, inside a call, inside an array, inside a template hole — only expressions are allowed.

A **statement** performs an action and evaluates to nothing. Six of them show up constantly in UI code: `if`, `switch`, `for` (including `for...of`), `while`, `do...while` and `try`. All six are fully supported — they run inside a `function` body, a lambda written with braces, or an `$effect` callback.

Mix the two up and the parser stops you and names the construct. Write `view = if (…)` and the error reads: `if` is a statement, not an expression — followed by the replacement to use.

code.caption: statements inside the body, an expression on the right of =

parts.text: The whole line is an assignment statement. A program is a list of these.
Everything to the right of this has to be a value. A statement here is a parse error.
A comparison. It evaluates to true or false, so it is welcome on either side.
The only branch that produces a value. Both arms must be expressions too.

tips: `for...of`, `for...in` and the classic three-part `for` are all statements — the loop keyword is what matters, not its shape.

Five of the six get the named diagnostic (`if`, `for`, `switch`, `while`, `try`). `do...while` in expression position falls out as a plain `Unexpected token Keyword "do"` — same rule, blunter message.

tips.text: `let`, `const` and `var` are optional in Aktion and change nothing about this rule. `let x = if (c) {…}` fails exactly the same way.

challenge.prompt: Each line tries to pick a view for the current tab. Three of them are parse errors. Which line does the parser accept?

options.detail: The habit from every imperative language. `if` runs a branch; it never hands a value back.

A loop evaluates to nothing at all. `.map` is the one that returns the array you wanted.

hints: Three of these open with a keyword. The one that parses opens with a value.
Finish the sentence for each line: "the value of this is …". Three of them have no ending.
stages.explain: The parser refuses `if`, `switch` and `for` on the right of `=` for the same reason JavaScript does: they have no value to give you. `if` picks a branch and runs it; `for` runs a body N times; neither one hands anything back to the assignment waiting on the left. A ternary is a different animal — it *is* an expression, so it evaluates to whichever arm it picks, and that value lands in `view`. Because the diagnostic names both the construct and its replacement, this is a mistake you get to make exactly once.

codex.def: An expression evaluates to a value and may sit anywhere a value is expected. A statement performs an action and may only sit in a body — a `function`, a braced lambda, or an `$effect`.

stages.title: The three replacements
stages.goal: Turn each rejected statement into the expression that replaces it.

teach.text:
Every rejected form has a shorter replacement. Learn the three and the restriction stops costing you anything.

A **ternary** replaces `if`. Both arms are expressions, so they can be component calls, and you can chain them (`a ? x : b ? y : z`) when there are three cases.

**`.map`** replaces `for`. It is *the* idiom for turning data into UI — `$rows.map(r => Row([Text(r.title)]))` gives you the array that `Column` and `Grid` already expect. `.filter`, `.reduce` and `.flatMap` are all there too.

For genuine multi-way dispatch, **wrap the `switch` in a function** and `return` from each arm. A function call is an expression, so `view = viewFor($tab)` is perfectly legal — and the `switch` never leaves the body it belongs in. That last move is the general escape hatch: any statement can produce a value if you put it in a function and `return`.

code.src:
banner = $error ? Callout($error, { tone: "danger" }) : Callout("All clear", { tone: "success" })
rows   = $orders.map(o => Text(o.title))
code.caption: ternary for the branch, .map for the loop

code2.caption: the switch stays in a body; the call is the expression

infographic.title: Rejected, and what replaces it
rows: x = for (let r of rows) { Row(r) }
function pick(v) { switch … } then x = pick(v)
return from inside a function body, then call it

tips: Chained ternaries stay readable for two or three cases. Past that, reach for the wrapped `switch`.

tips.text: `.forEach` returns `undefined`. If you want nodes back it has to be `.map`.

challenge.title: Rewrite all three
challenge.prompt: The same three branches, written as expressions. Fill each slot. Three chips in the bank are the statement forms you are replacing — leave those where they are.

hints: The two-character branch is `?` then `:` — condition first, then the true arm, then the false arm.
One array method returns a new array; the other returns nothing. You need the one that returns.
The last slot is the statement you are *allowed* to keep, because it is already inside a function body.
stages.explain: Nothing was lost in the rewrite. The ternary branches, `.map` loops, and the `switch` survives completely untouched — it just moved into a body where statements are legal, and the call `viewFor($tab)` became the expression that carries its result out. Note what makes the third one work: `return`. A `switch` cannot produce a value, but the function around it can, and a call is always an expression.

stages.title: Where a line ends
stages.goal: Know which leading token continues a statement — and which one silently starts a new one.

teach.text:
There are no semicolons, so the parser decides where a statement ends by peeking at the next line. If the first significant token there can only *extend* an expression, the line break is swallowed and the statement keeps building.

Those tokens are the operators: `.` `?.` `?` `:` `&&` `||` `??` `==` `!=` `===` `!==` `<` `>` `<=` `>=` `instanceof` `in` `+` `-` `*` `/` `%` `**`, plus the bitwise and shift operators. That is what lets you split a long method chain or a multi-line ternary.

**A `(` or `[` at the start of a line continues nothing.** Same rule as JavaScript's ASI. Break *after* the operator, never before the bracket — otherwise you end up with two statements that both parse, the second one does nothing, and not a single diagnostic fires.

  .filter(o => o.open)
  .map(o => Text(o.title))

label = "Subtotal: "
  + $util.format(total, "currency")

stages.title: The Gate
stages.goal: Route each fragment to the gate that will accept it.

teach.text:
Two gates. The left one is **expression position** — everything to the right of an `=`. The right one is an **imperative body**: a `function`, a braced lambda, an `$effect`.

Steer each falling fragment into the gate that will take it. Statements only fit through `{ body }`. Send one to `= value` and it shatters with the parse error you would have earned.

Eight clean routes clears the stage. Three shattered fragments ends the run.

code.caption: the value gate on the left, the body gate on the right

tips: Move the pointer (or drag) to steer the falling fragment left or right.

tips.text: In real code an expression is welcome inside a body too. The gate that matters is the one that *rejects* — and only `= value` ever rejects anything.

hints: Anything that opens with a keyword — `if`, `for`, `switch`, `while`, `do`, `try` — is a statement.
Anything with `?` and `:`, `.map`, `??`, or a bare call is an expression.
If it can finish the sentence "the value of this is …", steer it left.
stages.explain: The gate is not a metaphor for style — it is literally what the parser does. When it reads `x =` it switches into expression mode, and the only thing it will accept there is something that can produce a value. A keyword like `for` in that position has nowhere to go, so the parse stops and names the construct. Inside a body the parser is in statement mode, where expressions and statements are both welcome. That asymmetry is why every replacement in this world works the same way: move the statement into a body, and carry its result out through a `return`.

codex.def: Any slot where the parser expects a value: right of `=`, a call argument, an array element, a ternary arm, a template hole. Statements are rejected there and nowhere else.

stages.title: What the operators actually return
stages.goal: Predict the result of ==, === and < before you run them.

teach.text:
Comparison in Aktion is JavaScript's, coercion and all, because the runtime hands the operands to the engine.

`==` and `!=` are **abstract**: `1 == "1"` is `true`, `0 == false` is `true`, and the one you actually want — `x == null` — is `true` for both `null` and `undefined`. `===` and `!==` stay strict. Use `== null` deliberately as a two-in-one guard, and `===` everywhere else.

Relational `<` and `>` compare alphabetic strings lexicographically, so `arr.sort((a, b) => a.name > b.name ? 1 : -1)` orders correctly. `Date` operands coerce through `valueOf`, so `new Date(a) > new Date(b)` compares the instants rather than silently comparing two zeroes.

One documented divergence to keep in your head: **two numeric strings compare numerically**, so `"5" < "10"` is `true` in Aktion and `false` in plain JavaScript. Convenient when API data arrives as strings — surprising if you assume pure JS.

byName = $people.sort((a, b) => a.name > b.name ? 1 : -1)
newest = new Date($a.created) > new Date($b.created)
code.caption: one abstract guard, one lexicographic sort, one date compare

tips: `x == null` is the single place `==` beats `===`. Reach for it on purpose, not by accident.

tips.text: Relational `<` and `>` are the one corner where Aktion deviates from JavaScript: two numeric strings compare by value.

If the letter-by-letter rule ran first, `"5" < "10"` would be `false`, because `"5"` outranks `"1"`. It is `true`, so something has to run ahead of it.
One rule asks nothing at all — it just takes whatever the others did not claim. That can only be last.
stages.explain: `==` runs JavaScript's abstract-equality algorithm, which makes it exactly right once: `x == null` as a combined null-and-undefined guard. Everywhere else `===` saves you an argument in review. Relational `<` is the interesting one — each operand is coerced with the number hint first (that is what makes `Date` work), alphabetic strings then fall through to lexicographic order (that is what makes comparator sorts work), and one deliberate convenience survives on top: two numeric strings compare by value. Real JavaScript would tell you `"5" < "10"` is false. Aktion says true. Worth remembering the next time you sort an API payload that arrived as strings.

codex.def: Abstract equality against `null` is `true` for both `null` and `undefined` — the one place `==` beats `===`. Use it as a single guard for "no value yet"; use `===` everywhere else.

teach.text:
Everything from this world comes together in one small program.

`$tab` holds the current view. A `switch` decides which component to build — so it goes inside a function that `return`s from every arm, and the call becomes the expression. The grid arm builds its children with `.map`, because a `for` loop cannot hand you an array.

Two shortcuts are worth using while you are here. `$rows.length` works on any array. And reading a plain property off an array **plucks** it: `$rows.title` gives you `["Invoice", "Receipt"]` — exactly the shape `List` and `Col` want, with no lambda at all. `.first` and `.last` sit on the same path.

`default:` is the arm that keeps the page alive when `$tab` holds something you did not plan for.

And `List($rows.title)` is the array-pluck shortcut doing the work of `.map(r => r.title)`: reading a plain property off an array maps it across the items, which is why column-oriented components like `Col` and `List` read so cleanly.

outro.body: Expressions go anywhere. Statements go in a body. intro.headline: The binding is the bag, not the body
intro.body:
In every framework you have used, fetching meant three moving parts you owned yourself: a piece of state for the rows, a boolean for the spinner, and an effect to keep them in sync. Aktion gives you **one** binding that owns all three.

`$orders = $http({ url })` does not return the rows. It cannot — the statement finishes long before the network does. What it returns is a *reactive resource bag*: a handle whose `.data`, `.loading` and `.error` fill in later, and whose every field is reactive, so anything that read `.data` redraws itself the moment the response lands.

That one design decision removes `await`, `.then`, `isLoading`, and the dependency array all at once. What is left is deciding *which* branch to render — and there is a component for that too.
intro.code:
$orders = $http({ url: "https://api.example.com/orders" })

$app(Async($orders, {
  loading: LoadingState("Loading orders…"),
  error:   ErrorState("Could not reach the server"),
  empty:   EmptyState("No orders yet"),
  data:    Table([Col("Order", $orders.data.map(o => o.id))])
}))
intro.codeCaption: a fetch, four states, zero booleans

stages.title: The bag, not the body
stages.goal: $http returns a reactive handle; the payload lives in .data.

teach.text:
`$http({ url, method, headers, body, query })` is the base HTTP resource. `$query` and `$mutation` take the same config shape and differ only in *when* the request fires, so learning this one call teaches all three. The `url` is absolute — there is no `baseURL` and no per-call host default. `method` defaults to `GET`.

What it hands back is a *resource bag*. The binding names the request; the response lives one member deeper. Read `.data` for the parsed body, `.loading` for the in-flight flag, `.error` for the failure, and call `.refetch()` to run the whole thing again.

Every one of those members is reactive. You never copy `.data` into your own state — doing so is how the two drift apart.

code.caption: one binding, nine reactive members

parts.text: a handle carrying .data / .loading / .error — never the rows themselves
$query and $mutation take the same config shape; they differ in when they fire
the whole address every time — no baseURL. Cross-cutting headers go through $util.onRequest
the request leaves once, when the binding mounts

tips: `GET` is the default, so a read never needs a `method` key.

tips.text: `.data` is `null` until the first response arrives. Guard it with `?.` — or let `Async` do the guarding for you.

One row is the handle and one is the payload it carries. Telling those two apart is the whole lesson.
stages.explain: `$http` cannot return the payload, because at the instant the statement runs there is no payload — the request has not left the browser. The only thing it *can* return immediately is a handle whose fields fill in later. Making that handle reactive is what buys you everything else: when the runtime writes `.data`, every component that read `.data` re-renders itself, so there is nothing left for an `await` or a `.then` to do. The awaiting is the bag's job; yours is only to read the right member.

codex.def: What every Aktion data builtin returns: a reactive handle exposing .data, .error, .status, .loading, .headers, .lastUpdated, .refetch(), .cancel() and a settable .onDone. The payload lives in .data.

stages.title: Four states, one call
stages.goal: Cover loading, error, empty and data with a single Async(...).

teach.text:
A request is in exactly one of four states, and a real screen has to say something sensible in all four. `Async(resource, { loading, error, empty, data })` switches on the bag's own state and renders the matching slot.

The resource is the **positional** argument; the four slots are ordinary props in the trailing object. Leave a slot out and that branch simply renders nothing — it never falls through to `data`.

The slot worth the whole component is `empty`. It fires for `null` **and** for an empty array, which is precisely the case a hand-rolled ternary forgets. Pass `retry` as well and the error branch grows a Retry button.

code.src:
Async($orders, {
  loading: LoadingState("Loading orders…"),
  error:   ErrorState("Could not load orders"),
  empty:   EmptyState("No orders yet"),
  data:    Table([Col("Order", $orders.data.map(o => o.id))]),
  retry:   () => $orders.refetch()
})

tips: `Async` is a component from the Helpers group, not a builtin — no `$` sigil.

tips.text: Handed a plain array or object instead of a bag, `Async` treats it as already-resolved data. Handy in tests, confusing when you meant to pass the bag.

stages.explain: `Async` earns its place by making the four branches mutually exclusive *by construction*. You cannot render a spinner and a table at once, and you cannot silently fall through to `data` on failure, because the switch reads the bag's own state rather than a boolean you maintained. The `empty` slot is the real payoff: a request that succeeds with `[]` is a success, so `loading` is false and `error` is null, and every hand-written ternary sends it straight into the data branch. The user then stares at a table header with nothing under it and no idea whether it is broken or genuinely empty.

stages.title: The binding is not the rows
stages.goal: Spot the single most common Aktion data bug.

teach.text:
Here is the bug that ships more often than any other in this language, and it is one character wide.

`$orders` is a handle. It has `.data`, `.loading`, `.error`, `.status`, `.headers`, `.lastUpdated`, `.refetch()`, `.cancel()` and `.onDone` — and nothing else. It has no `.map`, no `.length`, no `.filter`, because **it is not the array**.

Nothing catches it for you. `$orders.map(...)` is a syntactically perfect expression; the validator has no idea that `map` is not a member of a bag. It fails at runtime, inside the branch that only renders once data arrives — which is why it usually gets past review.

infographic.title: Why the binding cannot be the rows

tips.text: `$name = $http(...)` names the *request*. The response is always one member deeper.

tips: If a member reads like something you would call on an array, you wanted `.data` first.

stages.explain: This bug is common because it is *right everywhere else*. In plain JS, `const orders = await fetch(url).then(r => r.json())` really does hand you the rows, so `orders.map(...)` is correct. Aktion removes the `await`, and the price of removing it is that the statement has to return before the data exists — so the binding must be a handle and the rows must live behind a member. Note the token that is only cosmetic: `method: "GET"` is redundant, since GET is the default, but redundant is not wrong. The bug is the one that asks a handle to behave like an array.

stages.goal: Catch only the members that really exist on an $http bag.

teach.text:
A request has settled and its bag is spilling members. **Catch the real ones. Let the impostors fall.**

The entire surface of an `$http` bag is nine names: `.data` `.loading` `.error` `.status` `.headers` `.lastUpdated` `.refetch()` `.cancel()` `.onDone`.

Everything else falling past you is muscle memory from `fetch()` or a request library. Catch three impostors and the run ends.
tips: Move the pointer — or drag on a touch screen — to slide the bag.

tips.text: `body` is a real name in the data layer, but it is a *request config key* you pass in. It never comes back out on the bag.

stages.explain: The bag's surface is small on purpose, and deliberately *not* `fetch`'s. There is no `.json()` because the decoding already happened — `.data` is the parsed body, not a stream you still have to drain. There is no `.ok` because `.error` is `null` on success and `{ status, body }` on a non-2xx, which carries strictly more information for the same read. And there is no `.then` because a bag is not a promise: it is reactive state that mutates in place, so its readers re-render themselves instead of waiting on it. Every time you reach for a `fetch` member, that is the tell that you are still thinking in awaits.

stages.title: Three doors
stages.goal: Pick between $http, $query and $mutation on purpose.

teach.text:
`$http` is the primitive. Two specialisations sit on top of it, and the difference between them is *when* a request fires and *how often*.

`$query({ url, key, ttl, refetchInterval, refetchOnFocus, refetchOnReconnect })` is a **cached, deduplicated read**. Identical queries — same `key`, or the same method plus url plus query plus body — share one in-flight request and one bag, so four components asking for the same list fetch once. Add `infinite: { param, limit, mode, select }` and the bag grows `.loadMore()` and `.hasMore`; pass `gql` with `variables` and it POSTs a GraphQL document.

`$mutation({ url, method, optimistic, invalidates })` is a **deferred write**. It fires nothing on render — the request goes out only when you call `.mutate(overrides)`. `method` defaults to `POST`, `optimistic` applies the change instantly and rolls it back if the write fails, and `invalidates: ["orders"]` refetches every cached query whose key contains that substring. `$util.invalidate(keys)` does the same on demand from anywhere.

Two more read the same way. `$socket` and `$sse` return bags with `.status`, `.connected`, `.last`, `.messages` and `.close()`.

code.caption: a cached read and a deferred write that refreshes it

tips: `$query` is `$http` plus an identity. Without a shared identity there is no cache to hit and nothing to invalidate.

tips.text: `$mutation` on its own does nothing at all. If your write never reaches the server, check that something actually calls `.mutate()`.
