order: A second reader shares that bag — no new request

hints: One of the three never fires on its own — that is its entire reason for existing, so it cannot open the sequence.
A cache can only be shared after something has filled it.
`invalidates` only means something if something else is caching, so it belongs to the writer, pointing at the reader — and it fires on success, after the write settles.
stages.explain: The split is about triggering, not about verbs — `$http` will happily POST and `$query` will happily hit a search endpoint. What separates them is when the request goes out. `$http` fires once per binding, every binding, which is perfect for a one-off read and wasteful when four components want the same list. `$query` adds an identity, so those four bindings collapse into one request and one bag — and that identity is what makes `ttl`, `refetchInterval` and `invalidates` meaningful at all, since you cannot invalidate a cache that does not exist. `$mutation` inverts the trigger for a blunt reason: a read that fires on render is convenient, but a write that fires on render would POST again on every re-render. Hiding it behind `.mutate()` is not sugar, it is the only safe default.

codex.def: $query is a cached, deduplicated read that fires on mount (key, ttl, refetchInterval, infinite). $mutation is a deferred write that fires only on .mutate(), defaults to POST, and can carry optimistic and invalidates.

stages.title: Write, then refresh
stages.goal: Join a write back to the read it invalidates.

teach.text:
A write does not update a list. They are two independent resources that happen to point at the same URL, and the read has no idea the write happened.

`.onDone` is the join. It is a settable property on every request bag, and it fires each time *that* request settles — on success and on failure alike. Assign it inside the action, immediately after you fire the write:

That is the whole pattern. `$mutation` expresses the same idea declaratively with `invalidates: ["orders"]`, and `$optimistic(() => { … })` wraps a local write so the UI moves at once and rolls itself back automatically if the callback throws or the promise it returns rejects.

code2.caption: and the page that renders it

tips: `.onDone` fires on *every* settle of that bag, including a `.refetch()` — keep the callback idempotent.

intro.headline: Nothing happens until you say when
intro.body:
Everything you have written so far *describes* a page. An effect is the other half: a body of work the runtime runs **for you**, on a schedule you declare rather than one you manage.

The whole design lives in the second argument. `$effect(() => { … }, [...deps])` — the list says when to run, and the runtime handles the rest: mounting, re-running, throttling, and tearing down the timers and listeners you opened.

That list is also the strictest thing in the language. It accepts `$`-atoms and exactly five string tokens. Everything else — including the one that looks most reasonable — is a parse error.

stages.title: Run this, when that
stages.goal: Read $effect(fn, deps) and know when the body runs.

teach.text:
An effect is not a component. It returns nothing, it never appears inside a tree, and you do not call it — you *declare* it and walk away.

`$effect(() => { … }, [...deps])`. The first argument is the body. The second is the whole contract: a list of things that, when they happen, re-run that body.

Leave the second argument off entirely and you get `["mount"]` — run once, when the program mounts. That is the form you reach for to seed storage, register a global handler, or send a first analytics ping.

Effects are also *where writes live*. You may never write reactive state while the UI is being built. Event handlers, actions, lambdas and effect bodies are the legal places.

$effect(() => { $console.log($count) }, [$count])

$effect(() => { $seen = $storage.get("seen") }, ["mount"])

$effect(() => { $seen = $storage.get("seen") })

steps.note: the body re-runs for that atom

tips: `$effect` is a statement. Put it at the top level, or inside a component body — never inside a `Column([...])`.

tips.text: An effect that writes state costs a **full re-render**: every component body re-executes. Only top-level `$name = value` atoms get path-level tracking.

challenge.title: The life of an effect
challenge.prompt: You never call an effect — you declare it and the runtime reaches each of these moments for you. Tap the six in the order they happen, from first render to last teardown. The timeline in the teach panel is the answer key.
challenge.help: Each trigger is followed by what it causes. One wrong tap ends the attempt.

hints: Start where the teach panel's timeline starts and end where it ends.
The six are three pairs: something happens, then a body runs because of it.

stages.explain: Nothing runs at the moment you write it. The runtime registers the effect and then waits for one of exactly two things: a lifecycle moment, or a change to something named in the dependency array. That is why `$effect(fn)` with no array is defined as `$effect(fn, ["mount"])` — the runtime substitutes the default rather than treating the list as empty, so the body runs exactly once, at the mount step, and never again. The teardown half is the one people forget: `cleanup(fn)` is not something you call, it is something you *register* from inside the body, and the runtime runs it on unmount along with clearing the timers that effect opened. One trap has no step on this timeline at all — `$effect("mount", fn)` still parses, because nothing about the argument *types* is checked, so you get a silent no-op. When an effect never seems to fire, check the argument order before you check the deps.

stages.title: The list is also a throttle

teach.text:
A dependency array can hold more than triggers. Mix in a **modifier** and the same list that says *when* also says *how often*.

`"debounce(N)"` holds the run back until the trigger has been quiet for N milliseconds — the autosave and search-as-you-type shape. `"throttle(N)"` caps the rate instead of waiting for silence. `"every(N)"` needs no trigger at all: the runtime owns that interval and disposes it for you.

The body still does ordinary work. `$http({...})` inside an effect issues a request and hands back a **bag** — `.data`, `.loading`, `.error`, `.refetch()` — never the payload. Rate-limiting the effect is what stops you opening one request per keypress.

Drop the quotes and you are no longer passing a token — you are calling a function named `debounce`, which does not exist. stages.title: Only two shapes get in
stages.goal: Admit $-atoms and the five tokens. Reject everything else.

teach.text:
The dependency array is checked by the **parser**, before a single line runs. It is not an expression that gets evaluated — it is a static list the planner reads to decide what to subscribe to.

So it knows exactly two shapes. A `$`-atom, optionally with a path into it (`$user.name` subscribes to that field alone). Or one of five strings: `"mount"`, `"unmount"`, `"every(N)"`, `"debounce(N)"`, `"throttle(N)"`.

Anything else is a **parse error**, and the one that catches everybody is `route.path`. The `route` handle is reactive everywhere else in the program, so depending on it reads as obviously correct — and the parser answers with `Unexpected Identifier "route" inside effect dependency array.`

Track the URL through `$util.url` instead. It mirrors `route` — `.path`, `.params`, `.query`, `.hash` — and it starts with a `$`, which is the whole difference.

code.src: $effect(() => { $emit("track", { path: $util.url.path }) }, [$util.url.path])
code.caption: the same intent, written with a shape the parser accepts

tips.text: `route.path` is the mistake that looks most reasonable, and it stops the whole program from parsing — not just the effect.

tips: `$util.url.path` is a real subscription, not a workaround: the URL surface is exposed under `$util` precisely so it can be a dependency.

stages.explain: The rule exists because the planner has to know the subscription graph *statically*, at parse time, before any of your code executes. A `$`-atom path is something it can resolve to a slot and watch. A recognised token is something it can wire to a lifecycle or a timer. `route.path` is neither — the router handle is populated at run time by whichever arm matched, so at plan time there is nothing to subscribe to. `$util.url` exists as a `$`-rooted mirror of exactly that data for exactly this reason: it puts URL state inside the shape the parser already understands.

stages.goal: Feel the rule instead of memorising it.

teach.text:
Candidate dependencies are orbiting the `$effect` core. Tap one to admit it through the gate.

**Admit only what the parser would admit** — `$`-atoms and the five string tokens. Let everything else complete its orbit and drift away.

One illegal admission cracks the core and prints the real diagnostic. `route.path` looks perfect. It is the trap.

It is not asking whether the value is reactive — `route.path` genuinely is — it is asking whether the *written shape* is one it can resolve to a subscription before the program runs. That is why the fix is never "make route reactive"; it is "name the same data through a `$` path". `$util.url.path` is that path.

stages.title: Whoever declares it, owns it
stages.goal: Put timers and listeners inside an effect so something tears them down.

teach.text:
An effect declared at the **top level** is global: it mounts when the program parses and tears down on the next response.

An effect declared **inside a component body** belongs to that instance. The runtime mounts it on that instance's first render and tears it down — running its `cleanup(fn)` handlers, clearing its timers, dropping its subscriptions — when the instance leaves the tree. Two call sites means two independent effects.

`setTimeout` and `setInterval` are tracked by the runtime and cleared on re-plan or disconnect. That is a safety net, not a scope: a timer started outside every effect is armed again each time the surrounding body runs, and nothing removes it when a single instance unmounts. Put it in an effect.

`$dom.onResize`, `$dom.onIntersect` and `$dom.onMutation` need no ceremony at all — those observers are auto-disposed.

code2.caption: same interval, owned and disposed by the runtime

columns.title: Outside every effect
columns.note: Re-armed each time the body runs; nothing stops it when the instance unmounts.

columns.title: Inside an effect
columns.note: Mounted once per instance, disposed the moment that instance leaves the tree.

tips: `cleanup(fn)` is a name that only exists inside an `$effect` body — there is no top-level `cleanup`.

tips.text: Every timer tick is a **full re-render**: each component body re-executes. A duplicated interval is not just a leak, it is compounding work.

Ask what runs again when the component body re-executes — and what is left behind when the card unmounts.
The `$tick` atom only exists to drive a timer. The right fix deletes it.
stages.explain: `setInterval` sitting bare in a component body is outside every effect, so nothing scopes it. Each tick writes `$tick`, which is a full re-render, which re-executes `LivePrice`, which arms another interval — the cost compounds. And when the card leaves the tree the timers stay: the runtime's tracking clears them on re-plan and disconnect, not on the unmount of one instance. Moving the work into `$effect(..., ["every(1000)"])` fixes both problems at once and removes the `$tick` atom entirely, because the interval token *is* the trigger.

codex.def: In scope only inside an `$effect` body. Registers a teardown the runtime runs when that effect's owner is disposed — the program on re-plan, or a component instance when it leaves the tree.

Call it from any action, effect or lambda. Three names are reserved by the runtime — `assistant-message`, `error`, `route-change` — so pick your own.

No listener to register, no listener to remove — the effect is declared, and the runtime disposes it with the program. The same two lines with `route.path` in the array would not have parsed at all.

intro.headline: A whole app is still one program
intro.body:
Nothing you have learned changes here. There is still exactly one `$app(...)`, still one file, still no build step. What changes is that one of the values inside it now depends on the URL.

`$router({ ... })` takes an object whose keys are path patterns and whose values are trees. It matches the current URL against those keys **top to bottom**, stops at the first hit, and hands you back a single node. That node is ordinary — it drops into a `Column`, an `AppShell`, or straight into `$app`.

The URL itself is readable through a reserved handle called `route`, and writable through `$util.url`. Between those two you can put a page, a tab, a filter and a sort order all in the address bar, where a user can bookmark them.

stages.goal: Declare a route table with $router({ ... }) and mount its result.

teach.text:
A route table is a plain object literal. Keys are path patterns, values are the trees to render. `$router(...)` matches the current URL against it and returns **one node** — the arm that won.

That is the entire mechanism. There is no router provider to wrap the app in, no `<Routes>` element to nest, no registration step. `pages` is just a value, so it goes wherever a value goes.

`default:` is the catch-all. Leave it out and an unmatched URL renders `null` — a blank page that the validator is perfectly happy with.

stages.explain: The router is a matcher, not a container. It never renders anything itself: it walks your object, picks the first key whose pattern fits the URL, and returns that key's value. Because the value has to be a node, every arm calls its component — `Dashboard()`, not `Dashboard`. And because the result is just a node, there is no special place it has to live. `$app(pages)` and `$app(AppShell(nav, [pages]))` are equally valid.

stages.title: Patterns and captures
stages.goal: Write literal, parameter and wildcard patterns, and read what they capture.

teach.text:
Three kinds of key, matched segment by segment against the path:

- **literal** — `"/settings"` matches that path and nothing else.
- **parameter** — `"/orders/:id"` matches exactly one segment and captures it as `params.id`.
- **trailing wildcard** — `"/docs/*"` swallows everything left and captures it as `params._`.

Inside the arm that matched, the bare name `params` is in scope. It is reserved, like `route` and `outlet` — you never declare it. Anywhere else in the program, read the same captures as `route.params.id`.

**First match wins.** `"/orders/new"` and `"/orders/:id"` both fit `/orders/new`, so the literal has to be written *above* the parameter arm or it never gets a turn. Nothing sorts the table for you by specificity; position in the object is the priority.

code.src:
pages = $router({
  "/":            Dashboard(),
  "/orders/new":  NewOrder(),
  "/orders/:id":  OrderDetail({ id: params.id }),
  "/docs/*":      Docs({ rest: params._ }),
  default:        NotFound()
})
code.caption: literal above parameter, wildcard last

tips: `params` only exists on the right-hand side of an arm. From a component or an action, read `route.params.id` instead.

tips.text: A `:param` matches one segment, never a slash. `/users/7/edit` does not match `"/users/:id"` — it falls through to `default:`.

The captures land in one reserved object: `params` inside the arm, `route.params` everywhere else. `"/404"` looks like a fallback and is not one — it only fires when the user literally visits `/404`, so an unmatched path still renders nothing.

stages.title: The shell that stays
stages.goal: Keep a layout mounted across navigations and swap only the outlet.

teach.text:
A flat table rebuilds the entire page on every navigation — including the sidebar nobody asked to touch. An arm shaped `{ layout, routes }` fixes that: it matches as a **path prefix**, keeps the layout mounted, and slots the matched child into the reserved name `outlet`.

`outlet` is in scope inside the `layout` expression and nowhere else. Child keys are matched against whatever is left of the path after the prefix, and `params` merges the parent's captures with the child's. Layouts compose, so a settings sub-shell is just another `{ layout, routes }` arm inside `routes`.

Because the shell survives the swap, so does everything living in it: the sidebar's scroll position, an open dropdown, a half-typed search box. That is the whole reason nested routes exist.

Links are the other half. `NavLink(label, { to })` and `SidebarItem(label, { to })` both navigate through the runtime router — no reload — and both derive their active state from `route.path`, so there is no `selected` flag to keep in sync.

stages.title: Path Finder
stages.goal: Feel first-match-wins instead of reading about it.

teach.text:
A URL arrives. The router walks your table from the top and stops at the **first** pattern that fits. Nothing is ranked or sorted by specificity — position in the object is the priority, and this table is written literals-first.

Tap the arm that would win. When no pattern can match, tap `default:` — that is the entire job it has.

Watch the segment count: a `:param` eats exactly one segment, a `*` eats the rest.
tips: Wait for the URL to finish typing. Taps before it lands do nothing.

tips.text: `/users/7/edit` looks like it should hit `"/users/:id"`. It has one segment too many.

challenge.note: The table is written literals-first, so a literal beats a `:param` on the same path. Three wrong taps ends the run.

More specific, but listed second. The table is never re-sorted for you.

`default:` is the right answer more often than it feels like it should be.
stages.explain: Matching is a linear scan, not a scoring function, and that is a deliberate trade: the table reads top to bottom exactly like an `if / else if` chain, so you can always tell which arm wins by reading. The cost is that ordering is now your job. Put every literal above the `:param` arm that would otherwise swallow it, and put `"/docs/*"` last, because a trailing wildcard matches everything under its prefix and nothing below it will ever run.

stages.title: The URL is state
stages.goal: Read, write and guard the URL without breaking the parser.

teach.text:
`route` is reserved, always in scope, and reactive: `route.path`, `route.params`, `route.query`, `route.pattern`, plus `route.navigate("/orders/42")` for an imperative jump from an action. It is read-only and it is never on the left of an `=`.

`$util.url` mirrors the same snapshot — `.path`, `.params`, `.query`, `.hash` — and adds the writers. `$util.url.setQuery("tab", "billing")` and `$util.url.removeQuery("tab")` edit the query string in place, so a tab, a sort order or a filter survives a reload and pastes into a chat window intact.

`$util.onNavigate(({ to, from }) => ...)` runs before every route change — in-app navigation and browser back/forward alike. Return `false` to block, a path string to redirect, anything else to allow.

And here is world seven's trap wearing routing clothes: **`route.path` is not a legal `$effect` dependency**. That array accepts `$`-atoms and the five lifecycle strings, nothing else, so `[route.path]` is a parse error with your name on it. Depend on `$util.url.path` instead — same value, and it is reachable through a `$` surface the dependency parser accepts.

challenge.prompt: Four lines about the URL, and only one of them is right. Order them by how far the program gets: on top the line that never compiles, then the line that compiles and renders nothing, then the line that runs perfectly and quietly breaks *other* lines, and at the bottom the line that simply works.

hints: Only one of the four cannot be compiled at all. Place that one first and the rest get easier.
The dependency array takes `$`-atoms and five lifecycle strings, nothing else. Count the sigils.
`$route` does not exist, so that line renders empty the first time it paints. The assignment paints perfectly — and takes `route.path` away from every other line in the program.
stages.explain: The three failures fail for three different reasons, which is why they are worth separating. `[route.path]` is rejected by the *parser* — dependencies are a closed grammar, so you get a real error at compile time. `route = $router(...)` is rejected by nobody: it is a legal assignment that happens to shadow a reserved name, so the router still works and every later `route.path` reads a field off your table instead. `$route.path` is the reverse mistake — the sigil belongs to builtins and state, not to the router handle, so `$route` resolves to nothing and the text renders empty. Reserved names are worth memorising precisely because two out of three failures never raise a word.

codex.def: Reserved, always in scope, reactive: `route.path`, `.params`, `.query`, `.pattern`, and `route.navigate(to)`. Never declare it, and never put it in an `$effect` dependency array — use `$util.url.path` there.

stages.title: Ship the whole app
stages.goal: Write a multi-page Aktion program from an empty file.

teach.text:
Everything that is left is a finishing touch on the same table:

- `RouteView(pages, { routeKey: route.path, animation: "fade" })` replays an entrance animation on every change, and does what a real navigation does — scrolls to the top, moves focus to the new page, announces it to a screen reader.
- `Redirect("/login")` navigates and unmounts the rest of the subtree. Return it from an arm to gate a page.
- `Lazy(loadReports, { fallback: Spinner() })` defers an arm until an async loader resolves.
- `Link(child, { to })` turns any node — a card, a row, an icon — into a router-aware anchor, for when `NavLink` is too literal a link.

Two knobs live on the host page rather than in your program: `router-mode` is `"hash"` by default, which works on any static host, and `"history"` gives clean paths at the cost of a server rewrite. `scroll-restoration="auto"` on `<aktion-app>` restores per-path scroll on back and forward.

Now write the table yourself. `$app(pages)` is already on line one — references resolve across the whole program, so define `pages` below it.

pages = $router({
  "/":        Dashboard(),
  "/reports": Lazy(loadReports, { fallback: Spinner() }),
  "/admin":   $isAdmin ? AdminHome() : Redirect("/login"),
  default:    NotFound()
})

$app(RouteView(pages, { routeKey: route.path, animation: "fade" }))

intro.headline: Not all state costs the same
intro.body:
Every world so far has used one tier of state: a top-level `$name = value` atom. There are two more above it.

**Hooks** give per-instance state — `$state`, `$memo`, `$ref`, `$reducer`, `$id`, plus any `$name` hook you write yourself. **Stores** give app-wide state with no prop drilling. Both mirror tools you already know, so the syntax will not surprise you.

The price will. Fine-grained, path-level tracking applies to top-level atoms *only*. Every other write — a hook setter, an `$http` settling, a timer tick, an `$effect` write, an `$emit` — re-executes **every** component body in the app.

That is not a bug to route around. It is a number to know before you pick a tier.
intro.code:
$rows = []                        // one atom, path-tracked
const [tab, setTab] = $state(0)   // one per call site
cart = $store({ items: [] })      // one for the whole app

nodes.note: the readers, or all of them

Compose `$state` and `$memo` inside a component

stages.title: Five hooks, five shapes
stages.goal: Know what each built-in hook returns before you reach for it.

teach.text:
A function whose name starts with `$` is a **hook**. Call it at the top of a component body and it holds state for *that instance* — the same role React's `use*` convention plays, with the same rules.

There are exactly five built-in ones, and they map one-to-one onto their React counterparts: `$state`, `$memo`, `$ref`, `$reducer`, `$id`. All five names are reserved.

Two rules come with them. Call hooks **unconditionally and in a stable order** — slots are matched by call order across renders. And hook state **resets when the instance leaves the tree**; a remounted component starts from its initial value again.

Write your own with `function $useThing(...)`. A custom hook's body runs inline in the calling component's hook scope, so its `$state` and `$memo` calls attach to that component, exactly like a React custom hook.

code2.caption: your own hook shares the caller's slots

tips: `setValue(prev => next)` derives from the previous value; `setValue(next)` replaces it. The initializer runs once, on first render.

tips.text: Omit `$memo`'s dependency array entirely and it recomputes on every render — which is the same as not memoising at all.
A hook inside an `if` breaks slot matching. There is no lint rule here to save you.

challenge.title: What comes back?
challenge.prompt: Match each hook call to the thing it hands you. Two hand back a pair you destructure, one hands back a mutable box you unwrap, and two hand back a plain value — which one it is decides how you write the left-hand side.

right.label: A [value, setValue] pair — the setter also takes prev => next
A cached value, recomputed only when a listed dep changes
A stable { current } box — writing .current renders nothing
A [state, dispatch] pair for many related transitions
A stable unique id string, for wiring for / aria-* pairs

hints: Two of the five hand back a pair. One hands back a box, one a plain string, one a plain value.
`$ref` is the odd one out: it is the only hook whose write schedules no render at all.
`$id` exists so two instances of the same form never collide on the same DOM id.
stages.explain: Aktion could have invented its own subscription API for per-instance state. It deliberately did not. The five hooks map one-to-one onto `useState`, `useMemo`, `useRef`, `useReducer` and `useId`, so the rule you already carry — call them unconditionally, in a stable order, at the top of the body — transfers unchanged, for the same reason it exists there: slots are matched by call order across renders. The corollary transfers too, and it is the one people forget — hook state belongs to the instance, so it resets the moment that instance leaves the tree.

codex.def: The per-instance state hook. Returns [value, setValue]; the setter accepts a value or prev => next. Call it at the top of a component body, unconditionally and in a stable order.

stages.title: Deps, or derive
stages.goal: Cache a computation with $memo — and know when $util.derived is the better tool.

teach.text:
`$memo(() => value, [deps])` caches a computation and recomputes it only when one of the listed deps changes, compared shallowly with `Object.is`.

That list is hand-maintained, and that is its weakness. Read one more value in the body, forget to list it, and the cached value silently goes stale — no error, no warning, just a number that stopped moving.

So `$memo` is the right tool when the inputs are ordinary values: component arguments, other hook results. A shallow compare is all it can see, and that is all those need.

The moment a `$` atom appears in the body, prefer `$util.derived(fn)`. It has no dependency array because it recomputes from whatever atoms the lambda actually reads — add a read and the dependency set updates itself.

columns.note: No list to maintain — it tracks every atom the lambda reads.

tips: At the top level you rarely need either: `$open = $todos.filter(t => !t.done)` already auto-tracks every `$` it reads.

tips.text: Args are compared shallowly too — passing a fresh inline lambda as a prop re-renders the child every time. Hoist the handler to a stable binding when that matters.

challenge.prompt: Fill the four slots. The indent shows what sits inside what — the dependency array gets its own row because it is the memo's *second argument*, not part of the lambda above it. Two chips are what a React developer types on autopilot, one is an incomplete dependency list, and one calls the setter instead of passing it.

hints: Both hooks are `$`-prefixed. Nothing in Aktion is called `use` anything.
The memo body reads two things. List both, or the total goes stale the moment the lines change.
`onClick` wants a function to call later, not the result of calling one now.

Slot 3 sits directly in front of `(t => t + 1)` — what goes there is the setter itself.
stages.explain: `$memo` earns its keep when the inputs are ordinary values, because a shallow `Object.is` compare is all it can see and all those need. The moment the inputs are reactive atoms, the dependency array becomes a second copy of information the body already contains — and second copies drift. `$util.derived(fn)` has no array because it subscribes to whatever atoms the lambda reads, so adding a read updates the dependency set for free. Per-instance caching over local values: `$memo`. A `$` in the body: `$util.derived`.

codex.def: Per-instance cached value, recomputed only when a listed dependency changes (shallow Object.is). Omitting the array recomputes every render. For values built from `$` atoms, `$util.derived(fn)` tracks its own dependencies instead.

stages.title: Who owns this?
stages.goal: Place a piece of state in the right tier: per call site, or app-wide.

teach.text:
The same three characters mean two different things depending on where you write them.

At the top level, `$draft = ""` is one atom for the whole program. Every component that reads it sees the same value.

Inside a component body, `$draft = ""` is private to that **call site**. Render `Counter()` twice and you get two independent atoms — instance state is addressed by where the call came from, not by the name. Pass `{ key: id }` at a call site when siblings reorder, so the state stays attached to the right one instead of to a source position that just moved.

When unrelated components need the same value, neither answer fits — that is `$store({...})`. Non-function entries are reactive state; function entries are methods that receive the store handle `s` first. The handle is an app-global singleton with reference-stable methods, so any component reads `store.field` or calls `store.method(args)` directly, with no prop drilling.

stages.explain: Identity comes from the call site, not from the name. Two `Counter()` calls in the same tree produce two independent `$n` atoms because instance state is addressed by where the call came from — which is also the whole reason `key` exists. Reorder the siblings and source position alone would hand the wrong atom to the wrong row, so `key: task.id` pins the address to something stable. A top-level `$name` has no call site to be private to, so it is simply one value everyone shares, and a `$store` is the deliberate, named version of that for state no single component owns.

stages.title: Render Blast
stages.goal: Feel the cost of a write instead of reading about it.

teach.text:
Every write has a **blast radius**: the set of component bodies that re-execute because of it.

A top-level `$name = value` produces the smallest one the runtime can. It knows which path you wrote and which paths each body read, so only the overlap wakes up.

Everything else is opaque to that tracker and falls back to the widest radius there is — every component body runs again. The morph reconciler still patches only the DOM that actually differs, so nothing flickers. The cost is in re-running your code, not in repainting the screen.

Four component bodies hang off the root below. Read what each round needs, then fire the write with the smallest radius that still does the job.
tips: Radius zero is a real option — one of the five hooks never schedules a render.

tips.text: A wide radius is not a bug. It is a bill. Pay it where the path is cold and refuse it where the path is hot.

stages.explain: The point is not that hooks are slow. It is that they are *opaque*. A top-level atom write is the only write the runtime can attribute to a path, so it is the only one it can narrow. Everything else has to assume the worst and re-run every body — which is nothing on a settings panel and everything on a table that updates per keystroke. Pick the tier by how hot the path is, not by which API reads nicest.

stages.title: What the tracker can see
stages.goal: Tell a write the tracker can pin to a path from one that re-renders everything.

teach.text:
The rule is short enough to memorise: **fine-grained, path-level tracking applies only to top-level `$name = value` atoms.**

These five all trigger a full re-render — every component body re-executes, and the morph reconciler patches only the DOM that changed:

- hook setters — `$state`, `$memo`, `$ref`, `$reducer`
- `$http` / `$query` / `$mutation` lifecycle changes
- `setTimeout` / `setInterval` ticks
- `$effect` writes
- `$emit`

The fourth one is the trap. `$now = $util.now()` is an atom write and looks path-tracked — but written from inside an `$effect` it is not, and a one-second interval effect quietly re-runs your whole tree sixty times a minute.

tips: Prefer plain `$name` atoms for hot-path state. Reach for hooks when you need per-instance isolation and can accept the cost.

tips.text: A full re-render is not a repaint. Every body runs again, so anything expensive you left in a component body runs again too.

challenge.title: The one that wakes everything
challenge.prompt: All three tiers are on screen: `$user` is a top-level atom, `$draft` is an atom private to this call site, and `n` comes from a hook. Four tokens are marked. Click the one that, when it runs, re-executes **every** component body in the app.

points.tip: the hook call itself — it opens one slot for this instance on first render
a member write on a top-level atom, fired from a handler
the setter half of the $state pair, called with a new value
a read of the per-call-site atom this body renders

hints: One marker is a read, not a write. Reading an atom subscribes this body to a path; it never invalidates one.
One marker is an atom write, and an atom write is the only kind the runtime can pin to a path.
Two markers come from the same hook. Only one of them hands the runtime a new value.
nudges: A hook setter is an opaque closure. It cannot name the path it changed, so there is nothing to narrow.
Declaring state costs nothing. Look for the token that changes it.
stages.explain: The tracker can only attribute a change to a path when it sees both sides — the path a body read, and the path a write touched. A top-level `$name = value` from a handler gives it both. A hook setter hands it an opaque closure. An `$http` settle arrives asynchronously, long after any read window closed. An `$effect` write happens outside the render pass. And `$emit` leaves the application entirely. With no path to compare, the runtime falls back to the only safe answer available: re-execute every body and let the morph reconciler work out which DOM actually differs. That is why the choice of tier is a performance decision, not a style one.

afterCode.caption: same statement, two very different bills

codex.def: Every component body re-executes. Triggered by hook setters, $http/$query/$mutation lifecycle changes, timer ticks, $effect writes and $emit — everything except a top-level `$name = value` atom write. The morph reconciler still patches only the DOM that differs.

stages.title: State that outlives the tab
stages.goal: Write a global store that survives a reload.

teach.text:
Persistence in Aktion is a config key, not a code path.

Add `persist: "key"` to a store and its declared fields hydrate from `localStorage` on first render and write back on every change. `persistIn: "session"` swaps the backend to `sessionStorage`, which lives and dies with the tab. `history: true` — or `history: 50` for a depth cap — adds `undo()`, `redo()`, `clearHistory()` and the reactive `canUndo` / `canRedo` flags you can hang straight off a button's `disabled`.

`persist`, `persistIn` and `history` are configuration. They are never exposed as state fields, so there is no `prefs.persist` to read.

When you want to write a single value by hand, `$storage` is the namespace: `$storage.set(key, value)` and `$storage.get(key)` hit `localStorage`, `$storage.session.*` is per tab, and `$storage.cookies.*` takes `expires`, `maxAge`, `path`, `domain`, `secure` and `sameSite`. A missing key reads back as `null`.

code.caption: state, one method, two config keys

tips: The store binding does not need a `$` — `prefs = $store({...})` is the idiomatic form.
A method's first parameter is always the store handle. `add: (s, item) => { s.items = [...s.items, item] }` is called as `store.add(item)`.

tips.text: Function entries are methods, not state. Only the non-function entries are persisted or snapshotted for undo.

challenge.title: Write it yourself
challenge.prompt: Declare a store called `prefs` that persists under any key, holds a `theme` value, and exposes one method that sets it. Then render it: a heading, the current theme as text, and a button that calls the method. Everything hangs off one `$app(...)`.

mustWhy: Shared state starts with a store — `prefs = $store({ ... })`.
Add `persist: "any-key"` so the value survives a reload.
A store method is a function entry that takes the store handle first — `setTheme: (s, t) => { s.theme = t }`.
Nothing renders without $app(...).

hints: Non-function entries are state; function entries are methods. Both live in the same object literal.
`persist` sits beside `theme` inside the store config — it is not a second argument.
Read it back with `prefs.theme` and change it with `prefs.setTheme("light")`.
nudges: The method's first parameter is the store handle. Mutate through it: `s.theme = t`.
Use `$storage` only if you want the manual route — this task wants the store to do it.
stages.explain: The split between config keys and state fields is what makes hydration safe: everything in the persisted snapshot is state by construction, so the runtime can apply it blindly on first render without deciding what to skip. That is also why methods are excluded — they are reference-stable functions, not values, and a serialised copy of one would be meaningless. Reach past the store to `$storage` only for values that no component renders: a dismissed-banner flag, a last-visited path, a token. Anything the UI displays belongs in state that the UI is subscribed to.

codex.def: A global store whose declared fields mirror to localStorage under the given key and hydrate on first render. `persistIn: "session"` uses sessionStorage instead; `history: true|N` adds undo()/redo() plus reactive canUndo/canRedo. All three are config keys, never state fields.

preview.caption: live — reload the page and the choice is still there

outro.headline: You can price a write now
outro.body: Three tiers, one question: how many bodies re-run? Top-level atoms are the cheap tier and the sensible default. Hooks buy per-instance isolation and charge a full re-render for it. Stores buy reach across the tree. None of them is the right answer on its own — the right answer depends on how hot the path is.
outro.nextHint: Next: put this under load — lists, forms and data that change while you are watching.

intro.headline: The form engine ships with the language
intro.body:
There is no Formik here, no react-hook-form, no resolver package to pick. `$form({ ... })` is a builtin, and it takes exactly three keys: `values`, `rules`, `onSubmit`.

It hands back a **bag** — the same shape you already know from `$http` and `$query`, with different members. `signup.values.email` is what the user typed. `signup.errors.email` is why it is wrong. `signup.submitting` is true until your write settles.

The validators are builtins too. `$util.rules.required()`, `.email()`, `.min(18)`, `.pattern(re)`, `.asyncCustom(fn)` — composable functions of one value, stacked per field in an array.

This world is where the one-argument-form rule bites hardest, because an input has a lot of positional slots and only one of them is `value`.
intro.codeCaption: state, validation and submission in one statement
objectives: Read values, errors and submit state off the `$form` bag
Two-way bind an input and label it with `FormControl`
Spot the positional slot that silently swallows your binding
Match each `$util.rules` validator to the value it can read
Write a validated sign-up form from an empty file

stages.title: The engine returns a bag
stages.goal: Read values, errors and submit state off the $form bag.

teach.text:
`$form({ ... })` accepts exactly three config keys. **`values`** is the initial snapshot — also the shape `reset()` restores. **`rules`** maps a field name to an array of validators. **`onSubmit`** is called with the values, and only once they pass.

What comes back is not your data. It is a managed bag, exactly like `$http` and `$query` return a bag: `signup.values.email` is the live value, `signup.errors.email` is the message, and `signup.touched`, `signup.dirty`, `signup.valid`, `signup.submitting` and `signup.validating` are reactive reads you can put straight in the tree.

The methods live on the same object: `field(name)`, `touch(name)`, `validate()`, `validateField(name)`, `setField(name, v)`, `setValues({...})`, `reset()`, and `submit()` — whose alias is `handleSubmit()`.

The library's own examples bind it to a plain name, not an atom: `signup = $form({ ... })`. The bag's members carry the reactivity.

code.caption: three keys in

code2.src:
signup.values.email      // what the user typed
signup.errors.email      // the message, or undefined
signup.valid             // the last pass found nothing
signup.submitting        // true until onSubmit settles
signup.handleSubmit()    // touch all, validate, then onSubmit
code2.caption: one bag out

tips: If you already learned `$orders = $http({...})` then `$orders.data`, this is the identical move with different members.

tips.text: There is no `.data` on a form bag. Values live under `.values`, and only under `.values`.

challenge.title: Reach into the bag
challenge.prompt: Six reads off the one bag this form returned. The small note under each is the name that does **not** exist here — the mono line above it is the real member. Match each real member to what it actually hands you. Three of the six are booleans, and only one of those three is about a single field.

right.label: The text in the box right now — the input reads it to paint itself and writes back through it on every keystroke.
The message left by the last rule that failed on this one field, or nothing at all.
Whether the user has been in this one box yet. Set by touch(name), and by submit() for every field at once.
True while an asyncCustom rule is still in flight — the wait before the engine can even decide whether the form is valid.
True from the submit() call until an async onSubmit settles — the flag that keeps the button disabled.
A whole prop set in one call: value, error, name, onChange and onBlur, ready to spread onto an input.

hints: Every note names something from another library, or a shortcut that collapses the bag. The mono line above it is real; the only question is what it holds.
Two of the six are the in-flight flags, and they are not the same wait: one is the rules still running, the other is your write still running.
Exactly one of the six is a method call, and a method that takes a field name cannot be handing back a single boolean.
stages.explain: Every data builtin in Aktion returns a bag rather than the payload, and `$form` is no exception — it just has form-shaped members instead of network-shaped ones. That indirection is what makes `signup.errors.email` reactive: the input writes through `.values`, validation writes through `.errors`, and every reader of either re-renders on its own. Collapsing the bag into the values (the `signup.email` shortcut) would leave nowhere for the error, the touched flag, or the submit state to live.

codex.def: The managed form engine. Returns a bag: .values / .errors / .touched / .dirty / .valid / .submitting / .validating, plus field() / touch() / setField() / validate() / submit() / reset().

stages.title: Bind a field, label a field
stages.goal: Wire a form value into an input and wrap it in a labelled control.

teach.text:
Two-way binding in Aktion is a *value*, not an event. Pass a `$variable` — or a member chain rooted in one, like `signup.values.email` — as an input's `value` prop, and the input both reads and writes it. No handler, no setter, no `e.target.value`.

Every input also accepts `onChange(value)`, which fires with the freshly-read value on every change. Use it **alongside** the binding when you need to do more than write state — debounce a search, persist a setting, kick off a fetch.

`FormControl(label, field, hint?, error?, required?, for?)` wraps exactly one control with its label, and associates the two for you. `FormSection(label, children, helper?, level?)` groups related controls — reach for it instead of hand-building `Card` plus `SectionHeader`.

For the accessible `<fieldset>` around a radio set or a checkbox group, use `FieldSet(legend, children, helper?, disabled?, error?, required?)` instead; its `error` is a group-level message rather than one field's.

code.caption: label, control, binding, error — four props, no handlers

parts.text: label plus one control, wired together for you
the visible label — always a string
the `field` slot (its documented alias is `control`)
a member chain rooted in the bag: reads and writes it

tips: `onBlur: () => signup.touch("email")` is the validate-on-blur idiom — `touch` marks the field and validates just that one.
`FormControl("Plan", { field: Select(...) })` and `FormControl("Plan", { control: Select(...) })` are the same call — `control` is a documented alias for the `field` slot.

challenge.title: Wire the email field
challenge.prompt: Complete the labelled, bound, validated field. Three chips are things a React developer reaches for by reflex — leave those in the bank.

hints: The control is the library's plain text input, and its `type` is one of the documented strings.
The value comes out of `.values`; the message comes out of `.errors`. Same field name on both.
`signup.touched.email` is a boolean, not a message — it can never be the `error` prop.
nudges: Two of the four slots differ only in which bag member you reach for.
`TextField` is Material UI. The component here is the one-word one.
stages.explain: Binding by value is what removes the handler. The input reads `signup.values.email` to paint itself and writes back through the same path on every keystroke, so there is no `onChange` to forget and no state that can drift from the DOM. Passing `error` from `signup.errors.email` closes the loop the other way: the moment a rule fails, the message is already in the tree, because it is a reactive read like any other.

afterCode.caption: the shape to remember

codex.def: Labelled wrapper around ONE control; the label is associated with the nested field automatically. Optional slots follow in order: hint, error, required, for.

preview.caption: live — blur the empty field and watch the rule fire

stages.title: The second slot is placeholder
stages.goal: Recognise a binding that landed in the wrong positional slot.

teach.text:
Pick **one** argument form per call: one positional plus a trailing object, all-positional, or a single all-named object. Never split an object between roles.

That rule is famous for `Button("Save", "primary")`, where `"primary"` binds to the second positional slot — `onClick` — instead of `variant`. Forms are where it costs you most, because the inputs have long signatures and `value` is nowhere near the front:

- `Input(id, placeholder, type, validations, value, onChange, ...)`
- `FormControl(label, field, hint, error, required, for)`
- `SelectItem(value, label, disabled, group)`

So `Input("email", $email)` puts your atom in the **placeholder**. It parses. It validates. It renders a grey hint that happens to be empty, and nothing is bound. And `FormControl("Email", Input(...), true)` sets the *hint* to `true`, not `required`.

Whenever the prop you want is not the one immediately after the first, use the trailing object.

code.src:
Input("email", $email)                 // $email → placeholder
Input("email", { value: $email })      // $email → value

SelectItem("free", "Free")             // value first, then label
SelectItem("Free", "free")             // reversed: submits "Free"
code.caption: same call, different slot

columns.title: Silently wrong
columns.note: Positional 2 is `placeholder`. The validator is happy and the field is unbound.

columns.title: What you meant
columns.note: One positional, then a trailing object — which reaches any prop by name.

tips.text: Nothing in the toolchain flags this. The program validates, renders, and quietly drops every keystroke.

tips: Two positionals plus a trailing object is fine too — `Col("Total", rows.total, { format: "currency" })`. What is never fine is splitting one prop set across both.

challenge.title: Find the unbound field
challenge.prompt: This program validates cleanly and renders a complete form. One field silently ignores everything the user types. Tap the token responsible.

hints: Three of the four tokens are called correctly. Compare each against its documented signature.
`SelectItem(value, label)` — value first — so that one is right. `Select` takes its options as `items`.
Count the positional slots on `Input` before you get to `value`. There are four in front of it.
nudges: The bug is not a misspelled component. Every name here exists.
Which argument is sitting in a slot that expects a string of hint text?
stages.explain: `Input("email", $email)` reads like binding and behaves like a placeholder, because binding in Aktion is nothing more than which slot the value lands in. The parser cannot help: an atom is a perfectly legal placeholder, so there is no type to reject. This is the same defect as `Button("Save", "primary")` — a call that is structurally correct and semantically wrong — and the fix is the same: the moment the prop you want is not the very next positional, switch to a trailing object.

afterCode.caption: one positional, then a named object

codex.def: Arguments bind to a signature's props in order. `Input`'s second slot is `placeholder`, not `value` — so anything you want past the first positional goes in a trailing object.

stages.title: Field Assembly
stages.goal: Feel which validator can actually read which value.

teach.text:
A validator is a function of one value. `$util.rules` builds them: `required()`, `email()`, `url()`, `min(n)`, `max(n)`, `minLength(n)`, `maxLength(n)`, `pattern(re)`, `oneOf([...])`, `matches(other)`, `custom(fn)`, `asyncCustom(fn)`.

Two of those pairs are one word apart and read completely different things. **`min(n)` and `max(n)` compare a number.** **`minLength(n)` and `maxLength(n)` count the characters in a string.** Put `min(8)` on a password and you have written a numeric bound over a string, not the length check you meant.

A form is assembling itself below. Rule chips arrive one at a time — **tap the field each one can actually read.** A rule that expects an address has nothing to check inside `18`.

Rules stack, so a field's entry is an array: `age` wants both a floor and a ceiling.

code.caption: the board you are about to build

tips: Tap a field to attach the rule waiting at the bottom. Three wrong attachments end the run.

tips.text: `.min` is not `.minLength`. Both validate cleanly and one of them guards nothing.

challenge.title: Attach every rule
challenge.prompt: Each field takes only the rules that can read its value — `age` takes two. Tap the field the waiting rule belongs on.
challenge.note: Tap a field card to attach the rule waiting at the bottom. Three misses end the run.

rules.label: .email()
rules.why: wants a string that parses as an address.

rules.label: .url()
rules.why: wants a string that parses as an http(s) URL.

rules.label: .minLength(8)
rules.why: counts the CHARACTERS in a string.

fallback.prompt: The `age` field holds a number. Which validator enforces "18 or older"?

options.detail: `.min(n)` / `.max(n)` are the numeric bounds — exactly what a numeric age field needs.
Counts characters in a string — it would demand an 18-character age.
`required()` takes an optional message, not a bound.
`oneOf` takes an ARRAY of allowed values.

hints: Two of the five rules belong on the same field. Look for the pair that share a shape.
Ask what the validator is handed: a number, or a string of characters?
stages.explain: A validator never sees the field, only the value — so `min(8)` on a password is a numeric bound handed a string, which is not the length check anyone reading the line assumes it is. That is the whole failure mode: picking the near-miss rule leaves you with a form that parses, validates, submits, and guards something other than what you meant. `min` / `max` are numeric bounds; `minLength` / `maxLength` are character counts; `pattern` and `custom` cover everything neither of them can express.

codex.def: `.min(n)` / `.max(n)` compare a NUMBER. `.minLength(n)` / `.maxLength(n)` count characters in a STRING. Choosing the wrong one validates cleanly and enforces nothing.

stages.title: What submit actually does
stages.goal: Wire a submit that validates, writes, and reports — without re-checking anything by hand.

teach.text:
`signup.submit()` — alias `handleSubmit()` — does three things in order: marks every field touched, runs the rules, and calls `onSubmit(values)` **only if nothing failed**. Async rules built with `$util.rules.asyncCustom(fn)` are awaited before that decision, and `signup.validating` is true while they are in flight.

So `onSubmit` never runs on invalid values. Re-checking them inside it is dead code.

The write itself is a separate builtin. `$mutation({ url, method })` returns a deferred bag that fires on `.mutate(overrides)`; its accepted keys are `url`, `method`, `body`, `headers`, `query`, `optimistic`, `invalidates`, `gql`, `variables` — there is no `onSuccess`. The settle hook is the bag's own `.onDone`, and that is where the toast, the reset and any refetch belong.

While it runs, `signup.submitting` and `$save.loading` are the two flags that keep the button honest.

code.caption: form validates, mutation writes, onDone reports

tips: `ValidationSummary(signup.errors)` renders the whole error set as a panel at the top of the form — hand it the bag member directly.

tips.text: `action: signup.handleSubmit()` submits while the tree is being built. The arrow is not optional.

challenge.title: Build the submit path
challenge.prompt: Switch ON every line that belongs in a correct submit path. Leave the ones that are wrong, redundant, or from another library switched off.
challenge.help: Four of the eight belong. Every one of the other four validates cleanly.

switches.label: onSubmit: (values) => $save.mutate({ body: values })
switches.detail: $form calls onSubmit only after every rule has passed.

switches.label: $save.onDone = () => { $toast.success("Saved"); signup.reset() }
switches.detail: onDone fires when the mutation settles — the home for the toast and the reset.

switches.label: Button("Create", { action: () => signup.handleSubmit() })
switches.detail: Wrapped in an arrow, so it runs on the click.

switches.label: email: [$util.rules.required(), $util.rules.asyncCustom(isFree)]
switches.detail: $form awaits async rules before deciding; .validating is true while they run.

switches.label: Button("Create", { action: signup.handleSubmit() })
switches.detail: The parentheses call it while the tree is being built, not when the button is pressed.

switches.label: email: [$util.rules.required, $util.rules.email]
switches.detail: Each rule is a factory. Uncalled, you hand $form the factory instead of the validator it returns.

switches.label: $save = $mutation({ url: "…", onSuccess: reload })
switches.detail: React Query's key. $mutation accepts url, method, body, headers, query, optimistic, invalidates, gql, variables — and reports through .onDone.

switches.label: onSubmit: (values) => { if (!values.email) return }
switches.detail: Re-checking by hand. onSubmit does not run at all unless the rules already passed.

hints: Two of the four wrong ones differ from a right one by a single pair of parentheses — in opposite directions.
One switch names a config key that `$mutation` does not accept. Check the documented key list.
If `onSubmit` runs at all, validation already succeeded.
nudges: Compare the two `Button("Create", ...)` lines character by character.
`$util.rules.required` and `$util.rules.required()` are different values. One is a validator.
stages.explain: The engine's contract is what makes the wrong four wrong. Because `submit()` touches, validates and awaits before it ever calls you, `onSubmit` is a place for the *write* and nothing else — a guard clause there is unreachable, and a rule you forgot to call is a factory sitting in an array where a `(value) => message | null` should be. The two parenthesis mistakes are mirror images: one call missing (the rule) and one call too many (the handler), and neither raises a diagnostic. Reporting hangs off `.onDone` because the mutation, not the form, is the thing that settles.

codex.def: Touch every field, validate (awaiting async rules), then call onSubmit(values) only when valid. `.submitting` stays true until an async onSubmit settles.

stages.title: Forge one from nothing
stages.goal: Write a complete, validated, labelled form with no scaffold.

teach.text:
Everything is on the table now: the engine, the bag, the binding, the labels, the rules and the submit.

Write a sign-up form. Declare a `$form` with `name` and `email`, make both required, add the email format rule, wrap each input in a `FormControl` inside a `FormSection`, and give it a primary button that calls the form's submit.

Remember the two traps this world is built on: the binding goes in a **trailing object** under `value`, and every rule is a **factory you have to call**.

If the real Aktion language service is reachable, it checks your program for real and prints its diagnostics under the editor.

tips: `$toast.success("…")` is a fine `onSubmit` while you have no server to write to.

challenge.title: Write the form
challenge.prompt: Build a sign-up form: a `$form` over `name` and `email`, `required` on both plus the email format rule, each field bound and wrapped in a `FormControl` inside a `FormSection`, and a primary Button that calls the form's submit.

Declare the engine: name = $form({ ... }).
$form needs a `values` key — the initial snapshot of the fields.
$form needs a `rules` key — that is where the validators go.
Both fields are mandatory: $util.rules.required(). Remember the parentheses.
The email field needs $util.rules.email() as well.

A field is `FormControl("Name", Input("name", { value: signup.values.name, error: signup.errors.name }))`.
stages.explain: That is a production sign-up form: labelled, bound, validated, accessible, and submitting through one call — with no dependency beyond the runtime you already have. Nothing here is form-specific machinery you had to build. The engine owns the values and the rules, the bag makes every part of that reactive, and the components read straight off it. Point `onSubmit` at a `$mutation` instead of a toast and the same file is talking to a server.

outro.headline: The form library was already installed
outro.body: One builtin owns the values, the rules and the submit. One bag makes all of it reactive. One rule about positional slots is the only thing standing between you and a form that silently drops every keystroke.

games.title: Theme & Polish
games.subtitle: One program, six themes, zero hard-coded colours

intro.headline: The theme decides. Your program only names meaning.
intro.body:
Six themes ship in the box — `light`, `dark`, `corporate`, `soft`, `glass`, `modern` — and the host picks one. Your program does not get a vote, and that is the feature.

So you never write a colour. You write `tone: "success"` and `variant: "primary"` and `gap: "lg"`, and the active theme resolves each of those into a real value. The same file that looks like a bank on `corporate` looks like a frosted pastel app on `glass`, with nothing edited.

When you *do* want to brand something, there is exactly one place for it: a `$theme({ ... })` statement. That is the only line in an Aktion program where a hex literal belongs.
intro.code:
$theme({ name: "corporate" })

$app(Card([
  Badge("Active", { tone: "success" }),
  Button("Renew", { variant: "primary", icon: "circle-check" })
]))
intro.codeCaption: no colour in the tree — correct on all six themes

satellites.label: radius
satellites.note: xs sm md lg pill button input

satellites.label: gradients
satellites.note: brand, accent, warm, cool, success, danger

satellites.label: icons
satellites.note: your own inline SVG by name

objectives: Brand a whole program with one `$theme({ ... })` statement
Pick the semantic value over the hex, every single time
Write icon strings Font Awesome actually resolves
Keep a page correct across six themes and two reading directions
Know when `Styles` and `HTMLTag` are the answer — and when they are the bug

stages.title: The theme is a builtin
stages.goal: Rebrand a whole program with one $theme({ ... }) statement.

teach.text:
`$theme({ ... })` is a **builtin statement**, like `$app`. It is not a component, there is no provider to wrap your tree in, and it never appears inside one.

`name` selects one of the six built-in palettes as the base — `light`, `dark`, `corporate`, `soft`, `glass`, `modern`. Everything else you pass layers on top of it. Selecting a theme by name also loads whatever web fonts that theme needs to look like itself.

Only the **structured** shape is accepted. Every top-level key must be a token group — `colors`, `radius`, `font`, `spacing`, `shadows`, `gradients`, `zIndex`, `motion`, `fonts`, `icons` — or the metadata keys `name` and `direction`.

stages.title: Semantic, never literal
stages.goal: Pass meaning — tone, variant, gap — and let the theme resolve it.

teach.text:
Every visual choice in the library is an **enum of meanings**, not a value. You say what a thing *is* and the theme says what it looks like.

The ones you will reach for daily:

- `Badge` tone: neutral · primary · success · warning · danger · info
- `Pill` tone: neutral · activating · success · warning · critical · promoting · corporate
- `Text` variant: small · small-heavy · body · body-heavy · large · large-heavy · heading · title
- `Button` variant: primary · secondary · outline · ghost · link · danger
- `gap` and `padding`: none · 3xs · 2xs · xs · sm · md · lg · xl · 2xl · 3xl

A wrong enum value is a schema error you will see immediately. A hard-coded value is worse: `sx: { bg: "#10b981" }` validates perfectly and then looks wrong on five of the six themes.

code.src:
Badge("Active", { tone: "success" })
Pill("SSL activating", { tone: "activating" })
Button("Renew", { variant: "primary" })
Row([left, right], { gap: "sm" })

columns.note: Tuned on light. Muddy on corporate, invisible on glass — and no error anywhere.

columns.note: Resolves through --rui-color-success. Correct on all six, forever.

tips: `Badge` and `Pill` do **not** share a tone list. `Badge` is the solid chip: neutral · primary · success · warning · danger · info. `Pill` is the soft state chip, and its own scale swaps in `activating`, `critical` and `promoting` (it also accepts danger / error / info / primary as synonyms, so only the three state tones are exclusive to it).

Need the resolved value inside a computed string? `$util.style.token("colors.primary")` returns `var(--rui-color-primary)`, and `$util.style.alpha("primary", 0.12)` tints it — both still theme-safe. `.cx`, `.gradient`, `.clamp` and `.toStyle` round out that namespace.

tips.text: `Styles(css)` and `HTMLTag(tag, { … })` are documented last resorts, for markup the catalogue genuinely cannot express. Reaching for either one to set a colour is how a program stops surviving theme changes.

`Pill` is the *state* chip. A certificate that is still being issued is not `pending` in this library — check the tone list.
The gap scale runs `none · 3xs · 2xs · xs · sm · md · lg · xl · 2xl · 3xl`. A pixel value is not on it, and neither is `medium` — the token for that size is two letters long.

You promise never to say what the pixel is; the theme promises the meaning will always read correctly — right contrast, right weight, right radius, on whichever of the six palettes the host chose. That is why `"#10b981"` in a `tone` slot is a hard error but `sx: { bg: "#10b981" }` is not: the first is a category mistake the schema can see, the second is a legal escape hatch you are simply not supposed to use for this. The library cannot stop you hard-coding. It can only make the semantic path shorter, which it does.

stages.title: Names, not glyphs
stages.goal: Write icon strings the runtime can actually resolve.

teach.text:
The runtime loads Font Awesome 6.7.2 for you — into the document and into every instance's shadow root. Host pages add nothing.

An icon string is the Font Awesome name **with the `fa-` prefix stripped**: `"house"`, `"chart-line"`, `"sack-dollar"`, `"triangle-exclamation"`. The default variant is `solid`. For the other weights, either prefix the name — `"regular:star"`, `"brands:github"` — or pass `variant`.

One string, one rule, everywhere. `Icon(name, { variant, size })` renders a standalone glyph, and every `icon:` prop in the library — `Button`, `Badge`, `StatCard`, `NavLink`, `Banner`, `ListItem`, `EmptyState` — takes exactly the same thing.

Never an emoji. A name must be ASCII kebab-case, so a pasted glyph fails the check and falls through a legacy path that prints it as **plain text** inside the icon slot — no error, and nothing that `variant`, `size` or `color` can reach. It is text sitting where an icon should be.

code.src:
Icon("chart-line", { size: "lg" })
Icon("star", { variant: "regular" })
Icon("brands:github")

StatCard("Revenue", { value: "$48k", icon: "sack-dollar" })
NavLink("Profile", { to: "/profile", icon: "user" })

Icons are decorative and hidden from screen readers by default. Pass `label` when the glyph carries the only meaning in its slot — a tick that means "verified", a padlock beside a plan name.

tips.text: `Icon("fa-house")` raises no error at all. It is a perfectly good string; it is just not a name the icon font knows, so you get an empty box.

stages.title: Token Match
stages.goal: Feel what a hard-coded value costs when the theme changes.

teach.text:
Values fall in **pairs**. Each pair is the same decision written twice — once as a semantic token, once as the literal it happens to equal on today's theme.

**Always take the token.** Take a hex and the host switches to a different base theme, which is entirely its right — and the little preview card in the corner shows you what that costs.

Three flips and the run is over. Bank eight tokens to clear it.
tips: The two chips in a pair are equivalent right now. That is the trap — they stop being equivalent the moment the theme moves.

tips.text: `#10b981` really is the success colour on `light` and `dark`. On `corporate` success is `#16a34a`, and on `soft` it is `#5eead4`. Nothing warns you.

`sx.bg` accepts a raw colour, so this validates — and then ignores every theme after this one.
The universal `style` passthrough. Same problem, one layer further from anything the theme can reach.

hints: Both chips in a pair look identical, so you have to read them. A token names a meaning — it has a prop name and a colon (`tone:`, `variant:`, `gap:`). A value is the thing that meaning happens to resolve to today.
Let a pair fall if you cannot reach the right half in time. A miss costs nothing; a wrong catch costs a flip.
stages.explain: A hard-coded value is not wrong when you write it — that is the entire problem. It is wrong later, on somebody else's theme, in a screenshot you never see. `#10b981` genuinely is `colorSuccess` on `light` and `dark`; it is `#16a34a` on `corporate` and `#5eead4` on `soft`, and a badge that insists on the first one reads as a slightly-off green on four themes out of six. The semantic token is not extra ceremony over the hex — it is the only version of the decision that stays true.

stages.title: Polish outside the tree
stages.goal: Reach $head during rendering, and keep the translator binding intact.

teach.text:
Three parts of a polished page are not components at all.

`$head({ ... })` sets the document title, meta description, canonical links, Open Graph and Twitter cards, and JSON-LD. It is **reactive** — it re-applies when the state it reads changes. But it only ever runs when the renderer *reaches* it, which means it belongs **inside a component body**, above the `return`. A `$head(...)` parked at the top level of the file parses cleanly and never fires.

`dir="rtl"`, `"ltr"` or `"auto"` goes on the host `<aktion-app>` element, not in your code. The runtime reflects it onto the render root and the whole tree flips — text direction, flex order, logical spacing — with zero program changes. (`$theme({ direction: "rtl" })` exists too, but it is metadata only — it records the intent and flips nothing.)

`$i18n({ ... })` returns `{ t, setCurrentLanguage, getCurrentLanguage }`. `t(key, vars)` interpolates `{name}` placeholders and understands ICU plural and select forms. Drive `currentLanguage` from a reactive atom and the page re-translates itself.

code.caption: inside the body, above the return

tips: ICU forms work inside a translation string: `{ n, plural, =0{No items} one{1 item} other{# items} }`.

tips.text: Do not shadow the binding you destructured out of `$i18n` — usually `t`. A parameter or loop variable named `t` makes every `t("key")` in that scope call the local instead of the translator. This one *is* linted, as a warning.

tips: Per-route `$head` calls compose, with the later one winning. That is how a layout sets the site suffix and a page sets its own title.

challenge.title: The tab title never changes
challenge.prompt: This program renders perfectly. The browser tab still says the host page's title. Tap the token responsible.

hints: Three of the four spans are ordinary and correct. The fourth is the right call in the wrong *place*.
The page body is fine. Only the thing outside the page is wrong.
Which of these has to be *reached by the renderer* before it does anything?
stages.explain: `$head` is not a declaration the runtime scans for — it is a call, and a call only has an effect when something executes it. `$app(OrdersPage())` executes `OrdersPage`, so anything in that body runs; a statement sitting at the top level of the file next to the `$i18n` bundle is just a value the program builds and drops. That is also what makes `$head` reactive and route-aware for free: it re-runs whenever the component that contains it re-renders, so a title built from `$lang` or a route param stays in sync with no extra wiring. Move it inside the body and the same line starts working.

You need a `Badge` with a `tone`, a `Button` with a `variant`, and a Font Awesome `icon` name somewhere. What you must not have is a single hex, a `Styles(...)`, an `HTMLTag(...)`, or an `fa-` prefix.

This is the payoff for the whole world: a program you can hand to any host, on any theme, in any reading direction, and it stays right without you being there.

intro.headline: Clean diagnostics are not a passing grade
intro.body:
Every program in this world validates. `getDiagnostics` returns nothing, the editor shows no squiggles, and the page still does the wrong thing.

That is not a hole in the tooling. A linter checks *shapes* — is this a real component, is this prop spelled right, is this enum value legal. It cannot check *intent*. It does not know which currency your invoices are in, that a bracket on its own line was meant to index the line above it, or that you re-passed a value the component had already worked out for itself.

Six trials. Each one is a program you would sign off on in review. None of them behaves the way it reads.

The scaffolding is thinner here. The distractors are things you have already been taught are correct — in a different position.

stages.title: The work already done
stages.goal: Stop passing components the values they had already worked out.

teach.text:
A large part of this library's design is **inference**. The minimal call is already rich: a component reads its own arguments and picks the icon, the trail, the box, the layer.

So passing what it would have inferred is never an error — it is a *replacement*. You swap a derived value for a hard-coded one that no longer follows the data, and nothing anywhere tells you.

Two of these are worse than redundant. `Toasts(...)` in the tree is not additive: rendering `$toast.items` yourself makes the auto-layer **step aside**, so a mistake in your mapping means no toasts at all. And an `AspectRatio` around an `Image` that already carries `ratio` gives you a box inside a box.

The cure is not memorising every default. It is reading the signature before you reach for a prop.

code.src:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Orders", { breadcrumbs: ["Home", "Orders"] }),
  Toolbar([SearchBar("q", { placeholder: "Search orders" })]),
  AspectRatio("16:9", [Image(src, { ratio: "16:9", alt: "Warehouse" })]),
  Toasts($toast.items.map(t => Toast({ title: t.message, tone: t.tone })))
]))
code.caption: four lines of work the library had already finished

code2.src:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Orders"),
  Toolbar({ searchable: true, searchPlaceholder: "Search orders" }),
  Image(src, { ratio: "16:9", alt: "Warehouse" })
]))
code2.caption: identical page, and the toasts still appear

tips: `breadcrumbs: false` is the documented way to *remove* the trail. An array replaces it; there is no way to ask for the derived one back.

tips.text: `Toolbar({ searchable: true })` mounts a `SearchBar` at the *start* of the left slot and wires `searchValue` / `onSearch`. Your own `left` children are appended after it — so passing both gives you two search fields side by side.
Rendering `$toast.items` into a `Toasts(...)` opts out of the automatic layer. Get the mapping wrong and every toast in the app silently stops appearing.

Two of them describe a layer or a box that a second call would duplicate rather than add to.
The label is the seed: `"Revenue"` chooses an icon, `"Ada Lovelace"` chooses an illustration.
nudges: Read each right-hand card and ask which single argument could possibly have produced it.
The toast card is the one that talks about a layer stepping aside — nothing else in the list has a layer.
stages.explain: None of these components is being clever for its own sake — each is removing a decision you would otherwise have to make identically on every page. That is exactly why over-passing is dangerous: the derived value tracks the data, and your hard-coded one does not. Rename the page and a derived breadcrumb follows; a literal `["Home", "Orders"]` array does not, and no validator on earth can tell that the trail is now lying about where the user is.

stages.title: Formatting that lies
stages.goal: Make a table print the currency, precision and date you actually meant.

teach.text:
`Col(header, values, { format })` accepts exactly four format values: `text`, `number`, `currency`, `date`. Write `"datetime"` there and the validator stops you — this is one of the few traps in this world it *does* catch.

What it cannot catch is the column that formats perfectly and shows the wrong number. `format: "currency"` defaults to **USD**. An invoice table for a German shop validates, renders, and quotes every amount in dollars. Pass `currency: "EUR"` — and `locale` if you want the separators and digit grouping to match.

Dates have the mirror problem. `$util.formatDate(value)` with no second argument defaults to the pattern `"MMM D"` — `"Mar 12"`. No year. On a page listing three years of invoices that is not a formatting preference, it is a data loss.

`$util.formatDate` takes a token pattern (`"YYYY-MM-DD"`, `"MMM D"`) *or* a named mode (`"relative"`, `"date"`, `"time"`, `"datetime"`, `"iso"`). Those named modes are the ones `Col`'s `format` does not share — do not assume a value legal in one is legal in the other.

code.src:
Col("Amount", rows.map(r => r.amount), { format: "currency" })

Col("Issued", rows.map(r => $util.formatDate(r.issued)))
code.caption: both validate; both print something you did not mean

infographic.title: Every part of this line is a decision

parts.text: one positional plus a trailing object — never split an object between the two roles
the first slot is the visible column header, not a key into the row
a column of values, not the row array — Col takes one column at a time
renders USD until you add a currency code; no diagnostic knows which currency you meant

tips: `currency` is an ISO 4217 code — `EUR`, `GBP`, `CHF`. `locale` is a BCP-47 tag — `de-DE`, `en-GB`.

tips.text: `$util.formatDate(value)` with no pattern is `"MMM D"`. Always pass the pattern when the year matters.

challenge.title: Bill in euros, date in full
challenge.prompt: A German shop's invoice table. Issued dates must print as `2026-03-12`, and every amount is in euros. Three of the six chips are the mistakes that still validate.
challenge.template:
$app(Card([
  SectionHeader("Invoices"),
  Table([
    Col("Invoice", rows.map(r => r.id)),
    Col("Issued", rows.map(r => $util.formatDate(r.issued, {{0}}))),
    Col("Amount", rows.map(r => r.amount), { format: {{1}}, currency: {{2}} })
  ])
]))

hints: One chip is a format name that does not exist at all. One is legal in `$util.formatDate` but not in `Col`. One is the default you are trying to escape.
`2026-03-12` is a token pattern, not a named mode.
The third slot is a three-letter ISO code, and it is not the one the component would have picked.
nudges: Slot 1 is a `Col` format. Only four values are legal there — and the one that looks most descriptive is not among them.
If you leave the currency slot to the component, every amount on this page is quoted in dollars.
stages.explain: The default is the danger. `format: "currency"` had to pick *some* currency, and USD is as arbitrary as any — but arbitrary and silent is the worst combination, because the column looks flawless. `"money"` and `"datetime"` are both rejected by the validator, which is why they are the *safe* mistakes: you find out immediately. The one that costs you a customer call is the euro invoice priced in dollars, formatted beautifully, with a clean build.

afterCode.caption: say the currency and the locale out loud

codex.def: `Col`'s `format: "currency"` renders USD unless a `currency` code is given, and `$util.formatDate(v)` with no pattern renders `"MMM D"`. Both validate; both print something other than what you meant.
